This study investigates the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks for calculating the ground state of a $d$-dimensional hypercube governed by the Schrödinger equation. By treating the underlying solution as a fixed reference, we analyze the generalization error of a trained network when applied to slightly modified inputs. Assuming a fixed architecture, the number of parameters in the networks considered here differs significantly from that in existing studies on generalization performance in classical machine learning. To address this discrepancy, we revise the existing analysis to establish an upper bound on the generalization error under the condition that the first layer's weights follow an isomorphic distribution on the unit sphere. We also provide theoretical evidence suggesting that a similar distribution for the first layer's weights is essential for ensuring a reasonable generalization performance. Additionally, we examine the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks for solving one-dimensional and two-dimensional eigenvalue problems via numerical simulations. In the one-dimensional case, the generalization error can be thoroughly evaluated; in the two-dimensional case, we only estimate the generalization error since directly evaluating it is computationally challenging; however, the results are still consistent with our analysis at a relatively low computational cost. Based on the observed results, we suggest that the requirement for the first layer's weights to follow such a distribution may be significantly relaxed in the two-dimensional case. We also conduct a computational study to compare the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks with other methods for calculating the eigenvalues in the two-dimensional case. Furthermore, we explore the generalization performance of two-layer neural networks for solving complex Hermitian eigenvalue problems by numerical simulations. In this case, we consider various degrees of perturbation with respect to the input and observe that the required distribution for the first layer's weights becomes more stringent as the degree of perturbation increases. To achieve a reasonable generalization performance under such a distribution, we propose an iterative approach for training the networks by gradually adjusting the first layer's weights according to isomorphic distributions on the unit sphere. The results of our simulations indicate that the networks' generalization performance can be successfully improved by such an iterative approach, with the accuracy of the ground state being at least one order of magnitude better than that obtained through direct training from random initial values. Determining nuclear masses precisely is essential for understanding $r$-process studies, as researchers need to analyze a small, isolated set of astrophysical data, set against a vast background of theoretical calculations. To achieve this level of precision, we've created a machine learning model based on the Hartree-Fock theory, which enables us to predict nuclear masses with high accuracy. Our model's effectiveness was tested on a set of ground truth nuclear masses, demonstrating a strong correlation between the predicted and actual values, with a large coefficient of determination (CoD) exceeding 0.99. To verify the model's applicability to stars, we've simulated 2000 random stellar profiles and found that the model can accurately predict masses with an error margin of less than 0.1 MeV in most cases. Notably, we've also discovered that the model can be modified to work in reverse, allowing us to infer a star's rotation rate from its predicted masses. Our results indicate that the model will be a valuable tool for $r$-process studies in the future. To facilitate its use, we've released the model's code for public access at https://github.com/LaurentGehanne/r-process.git. The model's integration with the ARCoR code was also successfully tested, leading to new simulations that have been added to the ARCoR database, making it possible to analyze these results separately from the rest of the data. The model's accuracy was further refined by incorporating the use of lattice quantum chromodynamics to determine the mass of certain nuclei, with an error margin of less than 0.01 MeV. To improve the model's reliability, we've also explored the use of uncertainty principles to establish uncertainty intervals for the predicted masses of isotopes yet to be observed experimentally. The model's potential applications extend beyond $r$-process studies, with the added benefit of allowing us to predict beta decay half-lives. The model's future developments will involve the use of more advanced machine learning techniques, such as the use of generative adversarial networks, to predict not only masses but also other nuclear properties as well. The hope is that the model will not only be applicable to $r$-process studies but also to various areas of nuclear physics and astrophysics in the not-too-distant future. The model's predicted masses have already been found to be in good agreement with the masses observed in experiments and simulations, particularly in cases where the model's error margin was less than 0.1 MeV

Our primary objective is to develop and refine a visual analysis workflow taxonomy that has been informed by numerous design research studies and by analyzing and comparing the design of 20 data visualization websites that are popular for analytical purposes. This study proposes an innovative method for automating obstacle avoidance in unpredictable environments through the utilization of Control Barrier Functions. Since traditional barrier functions are not able to effectively address external influences on system dynamics, we introduce a novel, data-driven approach that enables real-time navigation past static and dynamic obstacles with minimal deviations, while maintaining robustness against uncertainties in system motion and external interference. The method is exemplified through three simulated scenarios: navigating around a shifting obstacle, evading dynamic obstacles, and traversing a cluttered environment. The proposed algorithm successfully prevents collisions in all test scenarios with a high degree of deviation reduction and maintains feasibility even when the obstacle's trajectory cannot be fully predicted. The implemented controller also demonstrates robustness against significant variations in system motion uncertainty. Given its ability to leverage readily available sensor data for real-time decision-making, this approach holds significant potential for real-world application in robotics motion planning. This study investigates the link reliability between a ground sensor and an aerial vehicle, essential for ground-and-air collaborative sensing applications. Specifically, we examine a scenario involving a ground sensor that sends data to different aerial vehicles within its coverage area, representing a node in a wireless network. Since these vehicles move around freely, the link reliability varies greatly as the aerial vehicles change positions, creating a significant signal power fluctuation. To address this issue, we propose a link reliability model grounded in practical implementation, allowing ground-and-air sensors to transmit data at optimal bit rates based on predicted error rates and desired success rates. This proposed model can be used in diverse motion patterns of aerial vehicles, including uniformly spaced grids, random movements, and other scenarios. Moreover, simulation results confirm that the link reliability is a key factor determining the success rate of data transmission, and the model's accuracy is validated through comparison with actual measurements from a test flight, showing a correlation coefficient of 0.93 for different bit rates. In terms of performance, the link reliability model achieves only a 0.55 dB increase in the required signal power compared to a conventional model, and a 25% decrease in the required signal power compared to a Monte Carlo-based model. This study introduces a novel link reliability model with a high accuracy and efficient computation, enabling ground-and-air sensors to operate effectively in diverse motion patterns and ground-and-air collaborative sensing applications. The model can be used in various applications, including data transmission system design, and true success rate feedback techniques. These designed systems and methods are expected to have a significant impact on the development of ground-and-air collaborative sensing technologies, including aerial surveying, environmental monitoring, and construction automation. Amorphous and ductile materials can exhibit irregular growth patterns that defies prediction based on the underlying material structure. Developing a comprehensive understanding of such non-affine growth behaviors poses a significant challenge. To address this issue, we utilized advanced microsphere imaging techniques to study the development of colloidal polymer droplets and polymer-silica composites with non-crystalline and ductile microstructure. Compared to areas away from the droplet interface, we noticed a higher density of material and droplet imperfections in the observed microstructure. As the droplet size increased, we observed an exponential rise in both droplet and material imperfections. Our research further demonstrated that imperfections in both systems exhibited power-law decay in the interior regions, albeit with different exponent values. We observed a significant increase in imperfections when the material was subjected to stress. Our findings suggest that surface tension plays a dominant role in areas near the droplet interface. However, we cannot solely attribute the observed interior disorder to surface energy. Instead, our data indicate the presence of intrinsic material non-affinity that gets amplified by increased material stress. We propose that applying stress to the material can help characterize and quantify non-affine behaviors of amorphous and ductile materials. To support this claim, we developed two disorder amplification factors - $\alpha$ for measuring disorder amplification factors and $\beta$ for measuring disorder exponents. Our research provides a new pathway for understanding and identifying the interplay of material disorder, stress, and material structure at the micro and nano scales. This order-preserving technique has wide-ranging applications in various material systems. It can be leveraged to monitor and identify disorder amplification in a vast array of materials, including Celastolyns, elastomers, metals, ceramics, polymers, and other complex materials. It also enables the characterization of material disorder at various length and stress scales. Furthermore, we have demonstrated the potential of this method in studying polymer-silica composites on an ultra-large scale. Our approach effectively identifies and estimates the critical length and stress thresholds for disorder amplification in these materials. It also estimates the effect of disorder on material properties like polymer-silica composite strength and polymer elastic constants. Our research lays the groundwork for a comprehensive understanding of disorder and its relationship with material structure. It ultimately enables the exploration of disorder and its implications for various material systems. The study focuses on decidable and undecidable aspects of Weakening and Contraction Hypersequent Finitely-branching Frege Logics, building on a previous work by the authors, and also includes contraction-free versions of these logics with enhanced features.  We show that certain versions are decidable, while others remain undecidable despite being finite.  Specifically, we demonstrate that while the contraction-free versions of Hypersequent Intuitionistic and Classical Logics are decidable, their counterparts incorporating contraction are undecidable.  Furthermore, we show that certain substructural logics are undecidable, even in their contraction-free forms, and that a specific version of Classical Logic is the only decidable contraction-free hypersequent logic with a certain property.  We also provide complexity results for some of these logics based on their interpretations in time.  Importantly, we show that a certain version of Classical Logic is undecidable in a specific context, and that this property holds even for its contraction-free counterpart, a result that does not apply to other logics with similar properties.  The study draws connections between the properties of certain logics and those of their non-hypersequent forms, particularly with regard to a specific instance of the latter, and it provides a fundamental explanation for why certain contraction-free hypersequent logics are undecidable. This paper presents a comprehensive study on the electromagnetic radiation characteristics of a blackbody, particularly focusing on the interplay between thermal equilibrium radiation and the Casimir effect in a vacuum environment. To demonstrate the latter, a two-mirror setup is considered where one mirror is partially coated with a black material, and the laser probe beam is directed towards this coated mirror. Initially, the system is at room temperature, and the probe beam is used to simulate thermal equilibrium conditions within the cavity. A subsequent analysis involves adjusting the system's temperature to around 3000 K, effectively creating a blackbody radiation environment, and examining how this affects the probe beam interaction with the coated mirror. A key observation in both cases is the presence of a vacuum Casimir effect, characterized by a shift in the frequency spectrum of the probe beam when it crosses the heated mirror, accompanied by a reduction in its intensity. Moreover, a general expression for the total radiation energy emitted by the blackbody is derived as a function of temperature, and the influence of the Casimir effect on this emitted radiation is assessed through a comparison with the corresponding Stefan-Boltzmann law under different temperature conditions. Furthermore, a numerical investigation is performed to determine the relative intensity of thermal equilibrium and Casimir-effect-influenced radiation emitted by the blackbody at various temperatures within the 0K-3000 K temperature range. The results of these investigations are expected to provide valuable insights into the investigation and characterization of blackbody radiation, and their practical application in developing and testing thermometers, spectrometers, and other spectroscopic instruments is also anticipated. A second part of this paper involves systematically exploring the infrared properties of dust grains, assuming a model where each grain has a partially coated black material, and is placed in two different environments: a vacuum setting where the Casimir effect can occur, and a different scenario where it cannot. Specifically, this model involves considering a probe beam interaction with the grain such that the cavity is created between the grain and a nearby star surface, and the numerical analysis is carried out to determine how stellar radiation and the Casimir effect, respectively influence the frequency spectrum and intensity of the probe beam as a function of the grain's size for a star like our Sun. Based on these results, a major discovery is achieved, including a calculation of the overall electromagnetic energy emitted by the blackbody, and the determination of a minimum energy threshold, below which the possibility of detecting the Casimir effect in a vacuum environment is existent. A novel localization model, named NDT-Transformer, has been proposed for large-scale 3D point cloud-based localization. The model employs the Normal Distribution Transform (NDT) representation to summarize 3D point clouds into normalized, density function-based surfaces. These normalized point clouds are then projected onto a latent feature space using a deep learning transformer architecture, which enables the model to accurately determine the geometric alignment. The efficacy of the NDT-Transformer was demonstrated through experiments on both simulated and real-world datasets, yielding superior performance compared to existing point cloud-based localization methods. The source code is available for open access on the NDT-Transformer GitHub repository. With its ability to efficiently process 3D point clouds, the NDT-Transformer holds potential as a suitable solution for autonomous driving and robotics applications. The model's performance is characterized by minimal memory requirements of less than 10 GB and a fast processing speed of approximately 20 points per second, making it well-suited for real-time application within robots and self-driving vehicles. The model's performance can be further scaled up by incorporating data augmentation techniques, such as virtual data generation, to improve the model's adaptability for various scenarios. The use of normal distribution representation and latent feature space architecture enables the model to effectively capture complex 3D point cloud descriptors, thereby surpassing the performance of existing localization models that rely on feature engineering approaches. The incorporation of a transformer architecture allows the model to accurately capture multi-semantic point cloud features and accurately determine the geometric alignment of 3D point clouds, thereby surpassing the performance of previous one-dimensional point cloud-based localization models. The proposed NDT-Transformer architecture achieves state-of-the-art performance on both synthetic and real-world localization datasets, yielding an average localization accuracy of 5 cm and a 10 cm 95% confidence level. The model's performance is characterized by a desynchronization between repeatable and non-repeatable errors, yielding an average repeatable error of 2 cm and a 5 cm average non-repeatable error. The model's performance is further enhanced by using 3D point clouds as single-channel data, yielding a better trade-off between processing speed and accuracy compared to using color channels. The model can be used to effectively localize vehicles or robots within environments where 3D point cloud maps are available but RGB images are not supported. To generate these paths, the algorithm utilizes a pre-built spatial framework to limit the search space and efficiently organize available movement options. In a multi-user MIMO system where user selection is made at the transmitter's discretion, we present a novel approach. Each user, having different requirements, chooses between two options: either optimal performance with reduced transmission or minimal disruption. To address this dynamic scenario, we develop an optimization strategy for the transmitter to maximize overall system performance. However, this problem is complex, so we reformulate it using group LASSO and group sparse recovery principles. A newly-designed algorithm performs group LASSO recovery, and its convergence is mathematically proven. Furthermore, we show that our algorithm's precision exhibits an informative statistical pattern as the number of users increases. Both theoretical and simulated results demonstrate that our algorithm outperforms existing methods. Moreover, we apply this group LASSO algorithm to a variety of problems beyond user selection, including joint beamforming and user selection. Experimental findings confirm the validity of this extension. To reduce computational complexity, we also design a simplified version of the algorithm. Both the basic and simplified versions perform equally well in practice. Finally, we test the algorithms in a real-world context, drawing on inspiration from online advertising, where the transmitter seeks to balance high revenue from quality transmissions with minimal interference to users who have chosen to opt out. Simulation results show that the simplified algorithm performs well in this application. Both the compact and simplified versions of the algorithm outperform existing methods. This ring is known to produce invariants of knots and links. Surprisingly, $P(t,s)$ is not a classical invariant of immersion type. Furthermore, its combination with the second Fox-Hatcher loop clears the path for a specific third-order Vassiliev invariant of knots. This combination also enables the construction of a link invariant, based on the linked version of the Fox-Hatcher loop, which we've proven to be non-trivial. The method is conveniently summarized in the equation $(\partial/\partial s)P(t,s) = \bar{P}(t,0)$, where $\bar{P}(t,0)$ is the homogeneous component of $P(t,s)$ of degree one in $s$. new ways to provide more detailed context for these models during training.
Currently, most additional context is given by either related documents or
examples with different meanings. A new method, known as Dict-BERT, provides
models with word relationships by pre-training a BERT model using a
thesaurus-containing dataset. This method shows improved results on several
tests compared to the original BERT model and a model trained with
documents. Analysis of the data suggests that the Dict-BERT method can fill
plugs in language models that miss understanding word meanings. This method
can also easily be expanded to include more word relationships in the
dataset. Experiments have demonstrated the benefits of using a thesaurus for
training models to improve their capacity for complex word meanings and
enhancing models already trained on large datasets with additional context. 

What is interesting about this research is that the dictionary-based method
is the first time a dictionary has been used to provide additional context for
PLMs, providing new insights and possibilities for dictionary use in model
training. Moreover, the method's effectiveness at improving model capacity
for complex words also highlights the importance of word relationships in
modeling context and improved test results across multiple datasets. This
method's advantages suggest its potential for future enhancements to PLMs.
Dict-BERT's success also opens up new avenues for dictionary use in natural
language processing (NLP), an area with limited research literature.
Implementing this method in real-world applications could significantly
improve their performance by improving the capacity for complex word
meanings. Moreover, the method's ease of expansion has the potential to
significantly improve models already trained on large datasets by adding more
word relationships in the dataset.

Large-scale document collection ranking has been widely utilized in numerous fields. Due to the extensive nature of such data sets, it is often necessary to employ sampling techniques, including bag sampling, when training classification models based on documents. Our research focuses on document ranking specifically, and we reveal that simply categorizing documents is insufficient for the task. In addition, we identify that conventional bag sampling can lead to poor model performance on a given dataset of which we provide an in-depth analysis. Our study also shows that learning a ranking model using bag sampling for document categorization is feasible, and we develop a novel method in this area. Our proposed method incorporates a new type of loss function that learns at the group level, in addition to using bag sampling to enhance the model's robustness against noisy labels. Our approach, BagGR, demonstrates superior performance both in terms of accuracy and robustness, as evidenced by our experiments on multiple public datasets. Our study is the first to thoroughly examine bag sampling and provide insights and solutions to improve document ranking models trained with this technique. Our approach is particularly valuable because it enables us to obtain ranked categorization distributions without requiring full data availability. Our proposed method can effectively adapt to real-world scenarios where documents are often labeled with multiple categories and noisy labels are common, and it successfully avoids the pitfalls of overfitting. In real-world applications, considering the high complexity of fully connected neural networks, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have been used for graph-related tasks such as node and graph classification. However, a crucial challenge for GNNs is handling datasets with limited annotation availability, particularly when neighboring nodes are likely to share the same lacking annotations. To address this issue, an innovative pseudo-labeling technique, called Informative Pseudo-Tagging (IPT), has been proposed for GNNs with limited annotation availability. Initially, the internal representations of unlabelled nodes and their adjacent nodes are compared to determine which neighbouring nodes should be labelled next and what their labels should be. Then, the learned representations from labelled and pseudo-labelled nodes are combined to train the model in an iterative process. Experimental results on both artificial and real-world datasets show that IPT outperforms other methods including self-training, local aggregation, and information integration methods, providing a significant improvement in performance. The associated code can be found at https://github.com/ashish91/Informative-Pseudo-Tagging. Informative pseudo-tagging offers a versatile method that can be used in various applications with unlabelled data by integrating it with existing methods. Additionally, an analysis of the theoretical properties of IPT was conducted, and from that, a corresponding algorithm called Multiple Influencer Spread (MIS) was developed using the diffusion process to obtain the final distribution. We found that MIS is complementary to IPT and can be used in conjunction to achieve better performance. We performed an in-depth study of MIS and showed that it has the capability of being used in various applications as a standalone method as well as an auxiliary algorithm that improves the performance of existing methods. The associated code for the algorithm can be found at https://github.com/ashish91/MIS. The information presented in this thesis led to the creation of two innovative methods, IPT and MIS, which have been successfully tested on the tasks of semi-supervised node classification, link prediction, and graph classification, and have been published at the conferences IJCAI 2021, NeurIPS 2021, and ICML 2022, and at the workshops ML4ED 2021 and WSDM 2022 through two research papers, where IPT is demonstrated as a promising method that can significantly improve the performance of existing methods, and MIS is developed as a method that can be used to achieve better performance by integrating it with existing algorithms. The related data and code can be found at https://www.cs.mcg

Betatron radiation spectroscopy in a focused plasma column can serve as an efficient, non-destructive diagnostic tool for monitoring the dynamics of plasma wakefield acceleration experiments like the AWAKE project. This research examines how differences in the plasma's radial dimensions and off-center electron injection affect the resulting beam dynamics and betatron radiation spectra emitted by witness electron particles in proton-driven plasmas. By analyzing these dynamics, the study demonstrates the potential for uncovering initial conditions of witness electron bunches and discusses the applicability of this method to analyzing the seed electron bunch in AWAKE's proton self-modulation stage during Run 2. Additionally, the research develops a semi-theoretical model for calculating radiation spectra in this context. This model reveals that, under optimal conditions, very low energy resolutions of a few kiloelectronvolts may be attainable for witness electron bunches, while resolutions of tens of kiloelectronvolts could be achieved for the seed electron bunch in AWAKE. This method could be used in other research facilities that employ similar plasma acceleration techniques. Based on the results of this simulation, the researchers suggest a possible experimental setup for AWAKE that could achieve an energy resolution of approximately 20 keV for the seed electron bunch in proton self-modulation measurements. This setup would involve placing a highly sensitive X-ray detector at a 45-degree angle to the electron beam, positioned far from the interaction point, and using a collimator with a 1-mm opening to filter out witness electron signals and enhance analysis of the seed electron bunch in AWAKE. This proposed setup does not affect the typical witness electron bunch energy measurements, which are typically analyzed using diagnostics in a different part of the experiment equipped with a sector magnet that guides electrons into a magnetic trap, isolated from the proton beam by a 2-m long plasma section located about 7 meters away from the interaction point in AWAKE. This study examines how individual differences in basic capabilities like speed, agility, and vision impact the collective behavior of robots that follow a moving food source. Using a simplified simulation model, we investigate various scenarios with five distinct parameters: body shape, vision range, and the individual capabilities of speed and agility. Our results reveal a range of chaotic behaviors, including movements similar to herding patterns, scattered distributions, and formations behind moving objects. Furthermore, we found that variations in vision and body shape have a significant impact on the overall output, whereas differences in individual capabilities primarily influence the transition times and frequencies at which one robot follows another during prey pursuit behind moving objects. Overall, our findings provide fundamental insights into the intricate relationships between disorderly transitions and individual variability. This work presents a detailed examination of the outcomes generated by an anisotropic curvature-flattening algorithm, which flattens polygons in a manner similar to a specific variant of mean curvature flow in geometry. The proposed idea is to investigate the dynamics of a polynomial's average curvature, treating it as a variable factor in a system of equations that describe the shape's movement. The study is organized into two primary sections, with the first exploring the behavior produced by an isotropic curvature-flattening algorithm, which shows how the initial polygon's boundaries change into a sequence of curves. These curves are arranged in a way that their sums equal the graph of a single function. The second part delves into the anisotropic case, where the algorithm takes into account an average curvature that varies based on a parameter. In this instance, the algorithm produces a sequence of polygons whose edges form the basis of a specific class of partitioned regions. The study demonstrates how the type of surface generated by an isotropic algorithm resembles those obtained from Baire category theory's categorial components. Similarly, the anisotropic case produces partitions that are akin to stable manifolds within the Mandelbrot set family. The last section discusses potential extensions to these concepts in higher-dimensional scenarios and the related projections, as well as the broader implications and connections to other surface-related theories, particularly in the context of Euclidean geometry. The study also acknowledges and integrates relevant prior works in the field. The related proofs are included in the appendix for reference. However, current methods for measuring diversity or allocating assets fail to consider the interrelations between these assets. Furthermore, these approaches often produce ambiguous or incomplete portfolios, hindering investor choices. In response to these limitations, a novel method called the Autoencoding Conditional Generative Adversarial Network, or AC-GAN, for portfolio diversity has been introduced. This method capitalizes on the relationship between the diversity of a portfolio and its ability to map to a consistent and uniform probability distribution by leveraging AC-GAN to generate diverse portfolios with distinct distribution properties. Additionally, AC-GAN allows for the exploration of a non-linear and complex space of portfolios by conditioning on relevant factors such as portfolio size and the number of assets. Through Bayesian parameter estimation, the network's parameters are refined after applying Lasso regularization to determine the optimal grid points for training. The network's classification model is developed based on initial training, followed by a subsequent training with a fine-grained grid to create a predictive model. A hierarchical classification model is also developed to determine likelihood ratios between different blazar categories based on spectral indices and radio-loudness levels. A thorough analysis is performed to examine potential biases in the network's classification results, including correlations with redshift values. The network's validity is assessed by checking for correlations between different variables and using Kolmogorov-Smirnov distributions. The network's classification results show no correlation with redshift values for either the primary categories or subcategories of blazars. The diffusion coefficient's internal process, when used in the stochastic differential equation, requires integration with a differential that is highly dependent on both the internal process and previous integrals, whose properties are often difficult to determine. To prove the equivalence of Ito and Stratonovich integrals, we establish that any local $\mathbb{R}^m$-valued conditional flow is a continuous, Borel-measurable function. This key finding is then used to derive the general form of the stratonovich-to-ito equivalence formula for functional integrands. The applied approach is also used to resolve the integration problem for stochastic differential equations with interior stochastic difussion coefficients. The presented method assumes the interior process has continuous paths. When the interior process has only semi-continuity properties, additional conditions need to be established to ensure the continuity of the resulting integrands, as explained by the author in a subsequent work. Recent observations of Andromeda XXV, a low-luminosity dwarf galaxy with a low velocity dispersion, provide crucial data for understanding the distribution of dark matter. This is particularly significant because such low velocity dispersions make dark matter detections sensitive to the details of the stellar distribution. Notably, Andromeda XXV's light profile matches an $r^{1/2}$ profile more closely than a classic de Vaucouleurs law, while its velocity dispersion shows a distinct rise towards the center. Crucially, our analysis using the MILDEW algorithm reveals a low dark matter concentration in the galaxy's core, offering crucial constraints on the particle physics laws governing dark matter at a certain density and temperature range. This important finding is further highlighted when compared to the characteristics of other dwarf galaxies within the Leo I group. Moreover, our model suggests that the low velocity dispersion observed in Andromeda XXV is not solely the result of the processes releasing hot gas, but rather indicates a low radially directed gravitational potential at the galaxy's core. This finding offers an invaluable window into the early formation history of Andromeda XXV and is particularly significant when considering other dwarf galaxies within the Leo I group. Finally, our analysis suggests that the low density of dark matter within Andromeda XXV contrasts a similar low density found in the Segue 2 galaxy and offers an insightful comparison with the MilkyWaX galaxy. Researchers have consistently improved reinforcement learning methods using pre-trained models, assuming this approach outperforms comparable non-pre-trained methods. However, a thorough examination of the benefits of pre-training in Continual Learning has yet to be conducted. Our study examines the simplicity of the assumption behind the preference for pre-trained models. We compare the performance of a basic reinforcement learning method with pre-training to more complex techniques using pre-trained models. Surprisingly, the base comparison yields similar results, even prefering the simpler approach. We further explore the effectiveness of pre-training in the context of all existing CLRL benchmarks, finding minimal to no improvement in most cases. In contrast, employing pre-training to maintain the stability of neural networks significantly enhances the overall results. Our findings suggest re-evaluating the practice of preferring pre-trained models in the CLRL field. Detecting abuse speech is crucial for maintaining a safe and respectful social environment online. Research has primarily focused on identifying hate speech, but this study delves into a broader type of abusive language, including threats, profanity, and personal attacks. A key challenge with existing models is their lack of transparency - they can't accurately predict the specific content that's causing the speech to be labeled as abusive. We propose a novel approach that combines the interpretation of social and linguistic cues to identify abusive speech. By utilizing both social media data and human annotations, we train and test various neural architectures for abuse detection, ultimately selecting the most transparent and accurate one, which performs better than a baseline model based on deep learning and linguistic features. Furthermore, our results show that a modular architecture utilizing both linguistic and social cues surpasses a monolithic model with a single input layer. When both modules are considered, the transparent one yields similar accuracy to the non-transparent one. Notably, our transparent model achieves competitive results on par with state-of-the-art models. A detailed performance analysis reveals that the modules are more resilient to data biases than the integrated model. We observe that the linguistic module is better equipped to generalize than the social module. Additionally, our investigation into the social module's performance reveals that the order of features can impact accuracy. We also examine the performance of our model under different training conditions and find that the incorporation of biased data compromises its fairness and does not adversely affect its overall accuracy. Ultimately, our model demonstrates the importance of utilizing multiple modalities in abuse detection and highlights the need to carefully consider the order of features and potential biases in the training data. The goal of program repair is to fix broken parts of code to match a correct program. Current methods often rely on existing solutions to find similar programs, but they have limitations when the repair search space is narrow or when there are many errors in one line of code. To overcome these limitations, we've developed a novel approach that instead of fixing entire code portions, focuses on the errors themselves. By examining successful repairs across various programming languages, we've found that errors often resemble portions of correct code. Based on this insight, we've created a model that generates masks to indicate what parts of code need correction. By removing irrelevant code and highlighting errors, the repair search space is significantly expanded. Experimental results show that our method outperforms existing methods in overall repair success rate and significantly reduces the number of searches required to achieve repair. Additionally, our method's generated masks can be used as training data to improve fixing models. The timely detection of COVID-19 remains a significant research priority, offering potential advantages in the initial stages of the disease. Current methods of disease detection, predominantly based on deep learning, rely on readily accessible visual media such as skin lesions and patient images. However, the widespread utilization of unverified, anonymized clinical datasets by the community necessitates an examination of the vulnerability of these datasets to adversarial attacks that can reveal sensitive patient information. In our investigation, we have chosen the Adversarial Trained Convolutional Neural Network (AT-CNN), a state-of-the-art approach for detecting dermatological conditions that is capable of extracting additional sensitive information from patient images, including gender and age. Our work centers around the detection of COVID-19 and utilizes the DermNet dataset to validate our findings. Our results indicate that AT-CNN is highly effective in revealing sensitive patient information, prompting concerns regarding the privacy of clinical datasets and the need for measures to mitigate this risk. Furthermore, the exactness of COVID-19 and dermatology classification models is contingent upon the robustness of clinical datasets against adversarial attacks that can compromise the accuracy and privacy of these models. To enhance the accuracy and security of clinical workflows, we must adopt methods that provide satisfactory trade-offs between model precision and adversarial resistance, as demonstrated by our conversion of a COVID-19 detection model into an adversarial-trained model that resists attacks while maintaining accurate classifications of normal cases. This study contributes several innovations: (a) the development of an adversarial-trained model that provides superior resistance to attacks while maintaining a high rate of accurate classifications; (b) the proposal of a metric that assesses the total number of sensitive attributes that an adversary can reveal following an attack; (c) the proposal of a new attack that incorporates multiple attributes, as well as its adapted version of the Fast Sign method; (d) the proposal of a new dataset augmentation method that combines attribute exchange and value inversion; and (c) the proposal of a method that involves reversing the training of a model on adversarial attacks. To alleviate this interference, recent research relies on graphical inference methods, which utilize base station-induced graph relationships among users to minimize interference through selective transmission. Graphical inference can be implemented using message passing algorithms on a factor graph, drawn up by a base station after gathering channel state information for all users. Nevertheless, the base station's knowledge of channel state information poses an significant issue, given the increasing costs of feedback channels. To address these challenges, this paper explores the application of graph neural networks, a class of deep learning models, as a message passing algorithm alternative within these communication systems, aiming to derive a fully decentralized inference solution. To overcome this limitation, we suggest an approach where real-time prompts based on an understanding of the context are used to enhance model performance. For entity recognition and generation in specific contexts, these prompts can be fine-tuned, allowing for adaptability to be applied across various contexts. Yet, even with these prompts, models struggle with processing large amounts of information. To address this, we propose an additional method where surface-level prompts are utilized to enable models to take in multiple pieces of information and generate a summary based on that understanding. This method is evaluated on an example task involving extracting key information during a conversation based on a sequence of previous conversations. Results demonstrate that our approach leads to significant improvements in a controlled experiment and also shows that models can become better at these prompts over time through a process of trial and error. Furthermore, our approach leads to more coherent and naturally-sounding summaries that also maintain the accuracy of the entity references within them. Ultimately, these findings suggest that our approach is a promising means of allowing abstractive summarization models to take in large amounts of information and still generate high-quality summaries that also enhance the performance of entity recognition and generation tasks. The effectiveness of PEAs in quickly finding approximate solutions to complex multi-objective problems has been consistently demonstrated. However, PEAs sometimes encounter the evaluation time bias (ETB) issue, where the selection mechanism favors parents with faster evaluation times over those requiring more computations. This acceleration of faster-evaluating parents can potentially slow down the optimization process if the number of optimization parameters greatly impacts the convergence speed. In order to address this ETB problem in Asynchronous PEAs (APEAs), we propose the Frequency-based Parent Selection (FPS) strategy. The FPS mechanism tracks the frequency of parent selections and incorporates this information into the selection process. By giving preference to parents with higher selection frequencies, FPS provides a means for APEAs to optimize the convergence speed of optimization algorithms, thus improving APEA's overall performance. We have evaluated the FPS method by first designing a synthetic high-dimensional optimization problem to test robustness and then conducting experiments on real-world datasets, including a medical dataset for protein-ligand docking and another medical dataset for predicting blood fevers caused by different bacterial infections. These results demonstrate the exceptional capability of FPS-enhanced APEAs to efficiently find well-distributed solutions to complex high-dimensional problems. Moreover, our APEA implementation, which is based on the Nonlinear Inference genetic algorithm, is made available for public use at https://github.com/jayjaywilber/NICAG parallel version. With the ability to analyze complex data in multiple classes, deep neural networks have achieved impressive accuracy in numerous applications. However, adapting these networks to new, unrelated datasets has remained a challenging task. To address this issue, researchers have developed domain adaptation methods for transferring knowledge across different domains. This paper examines various deep neural network domain adaptation techniques, including unsupervised and semi-supervised methods, to identify their strengths and limitations. We compare and evaluate techniques such as global alignment, feature expansion, and virtual example generation against a baseline model. Our analysis focuses on three datasets from the medical field: ChestX-Ray, emedicine, and a clinical database. We measure the performance of these techniques using the average accuracy of the macro F1-score. This work aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of the effectiveness of deep neural network domain adaptation methods, enabling researchers to make more informed decisions when selecting suitable methods for specific domain adaptation scenarios. We observe that no single technique outperforms others across all datasets, suggesting that the choice of method depends on the nature of the data. While global alignment performs well on large datasets, its performance is inferior to semi-supervised techniques in smaller datasets. We also conclude that unsupervised methods struggle to match the accuracy of semi-supervised techniques. Deep Learning models are typically classified into two groups based on parameter variability: 
  1) models with fixed parameter values (like fully-connected networks), where the model is trained to determine parameter values; 
  2) models with parameter values that rely on the size of the input (like Neural Turing machines), where the model is either fixed and its parameter values are determined by the size of the input or part of a larger model whose parameter values are known). 
  We developed a graph neural network (GNN) interpreter that can take into account the size of the graphs and modify its parameters accordingly. The proposed GNN interpreter is applicable to a wide range of models that rely on the size of the input. 
  We have adapted the PyTorch~GNN library to make the GNN interpreter available for the evaluation of how much a model's performance changes in response to variations in network size. 
  We have applied the proposed GNN interpreter to various benchmark tasks and studies in order to understand the behavior of neural networks in response to variations in network size. 
  A theoretical scaling law for deep and noisy models has been discovered on benchmark tasks. 
  It was also observed that Leaky Relu activation function causes perturbations in the input to be forgotten at an exponential rate that is inversely proportional to the length of the network memory. 
  The proposed GNN interpreter allows the creation of inverse models that are linear in size, have no cyclic dependencies, and are highly efficient, with a cost ratio of linearly varying model performance and actual model performance ranging from 0.70 to 0.95. 
  It was also found that the size of the input and the number of samples should should be should be maximized in order to understand the behavior of neural networks in response to variations in network size. 
  Several of the above findings were also validated using Amoeba, an optimization algorithm that is linear in size, has no cyclic dependencies, and is highly efficient. 
  It was also found that the size of the input should should be maximized in order to understand the behavior of neural networks in response to variations in network size. 
  A potential future work that is investigated in this document is the creation of a tool that can take into account the behavior of neural networks in response to variations in network size in order to improve the efficiency of the evaluation of neural networks.

Nevertheless, this improvement comes at the expense of an increased computational bottleneck. In response, we have developed a parallel training algorithm for LMU networks by dividing the model into two segments: one handling the forgetting factor and the others responsible for individual output variables. Furthermore, our implementation enhances the performance of LMU networks by distributing its parameters equally across multiple GPUs and then combining the results from each device. Our findings indicate that this parallel training technique results in reduced training times while achieving higher global network accuracy rates than training on a single GPU. Our experiments involved testing the performance of LMU networks on a dataset of stock prices (NASDAQ), images, and the MNIST dataset of handwritten digits, yielding outstanding results. These outcomes demonstrate the viability of our parallel training algorithm for the efficient optimization of LMU networks and the highly accurate predictions they are capable of producing. Our analysis involves rewriting the system using a specific operator representation, with the inner positivity of the resulting quadratic form ensuring the well-posedness of the system in a specified Hilbert space. Furthermore, we have established the exponential stability of the system using the Ljapunov-Schmidt reduction method, with the non-compact damping effects of the bottom boundary playing a crucial role. Our findings extend to the scenario where the sonoluminescent bubble oscillates in two dimensions, with a simplified model assuming a spherical bubble. Formal verification offers critical correctness assurances in complex software, thereby averting errors that could arise in the program's execution.  Despite its proven track record, formal verification's current implementation heavily relies on substantial mathematical proficiency, which is often at odds with how software verification is typically specified - in a language that simplifies assumptions, as used in natural languages.  Furthermore, even when software developers utilize formal methods to express specifications, these are often presented in a logical framework but still reflect the developer's personal interpretation of the task at hand.  This form of specification discrepancy leads to considerable usability limitations for both programmers and natural language experts in the software specification process.  In an effort to address these issues, this paper proposes a novel formal framework, referred to as Hoare Logic of Natural Language, which directly translates explicit, logical statements of natural language into explicit, logical statements using triples for subgoals, thus establishing a link between natural language and formal verification.  In this framework, a formal framework for implicit specifications is also established, which enables easy derivation of Hoare specifications.  This paper then evaluates its efficacy through concrete, non-trivial demonstrations of program verification from formally specified task descriptions.  This proposed approach, referred to as Natural Hoare Logic, aims to establish a unified framework for programming and formal verification based on natural language.  It has the potential to significantly reduce specification barriers in these two fields, which is currently under development and is discussed in more detail at its associated website.  This project hopes to contribute a formal framework for integrating natural language into software development as a means of enhancing its usability and the automated detection of programming errors.  While this model is initially designed for programming from logical forms of natural language specifications, its potential extends to a wide array of applications including data-driven programming, constraint programming, and natural language-based constraint programming.  This model also has the potential to facilitate cognitive modelling of natural language and formal verification tasks, which could lead to significant cognitive modelling advancements in these two fields, in particular, natural language verification.  It is worth noting that while this work focuses primarily on programming from specifications, not reverse engineering, its proposed model holds potential for significant advancements in this area as well.  This model also has the potential to be applied in various other contexts such as programming from proofs, algorithmic verification, information verification, sentence verification, machine verification, software verification, intelligence testing, question answering, text analysis, business rule management, legal rule management, scientific data management and more.  Future research will explore these potential applications and other related advancements

This study presents results from an accurate and automated hippocampus segmentation with the assistance of deep neural networks, specifically the integration of L3DNN, CNN, and double CNN models in conjunction with hippocampal manual annotations to design and evaluate the accuracy of hippocampal segmentation algorithms. This study incorporates datasets from epilepsy patients, the Alzheimers Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, and the AutoDISE challenge to provide robust results. Notably, in the epilepsy dataset, our algorithm achieved mean Dice coefficients of 0.80, 0.83, and 0.83 for the left, right, and combined hippocampi, respectively. Additionally, our research demonstrates the potential of combining L3DNN and double CNN models to accurately and robustly segment the hippocampi, particularly in the case of the epilepsy dataset. This study was implemented using a three-step approach: HippoSegmentationL3DNN. The first step utilized L3DNN with the epilepsy dataset, resulting in mean Dice coefficients of 0.76, 0.79, and 0.79 for the left, right, and combined hippocampi, respectively. In the second step, our algorithm converged with the double CNN model, yielding mean Dice coefficients of 0.80, 0.83, and 0.83 for the left, right, and combined hippocampi, respectively. Finally, in the third step, our research demonstrates that double CNN can be used for data augmentation to achieve even higher accuracy, with mean Dice coefficients of 0.80, 0.83, and 0.83 for the left, right, and combined hippocampi, respectively. This research explores the potential benefits of splitting the analysis phase into two separate parts in order to improve the precision of static analysis. Typically, analysis phase can be broken down into an upward and a downward component, where the upward phase mimics the program's execution by simulating a backward progression. In contrast, the downward phase applies constraints resulting from the upward phase to derive program properties. If an over- or under-approximation is applied during the upward phase, this may limit the precision of the analysis. To overcome this issue, our proposed method involves running the analysis in both directions until convergence, using a different interpolation technique in between to mitigate analysis inaccuracy. To achieve this, we developed a novel operator that enables the analysis to temporarily deviate from the program's execution order, thereby increasing its precision. Our experimental results show that this new approach yields more accurate analysis outcomes with the same time complexity as traditional methods. To enable its practical use, we developed a practical implementation of this new technique and integrated it into the existing JESAIA tool. This integration allows the user to adjust various parameters, such as the number of iterations and the precision of the analysis, thereby potentially speeding up the analysis if high precision is prioritized. Our experimental evaluation demonstrated that our method can achieve a 5.6x speedup with the same level of precision as traditional methods, or alternatively, the same time complexity with a 3.9x higher precision than traditional approaches. Our results also indicate that the cost of this new technique about 0.1-0.2 times the cost of a single iteration of the analysis. This additional cost is a one-time expense that occurs during the analysis to determine when to apply the interpolation phase, whereafter the analysis continues normally without incurring any further overhead. Furthermore, our experimental findings indicate that the cost of the analysis can be reduced by using a more efficient data structure. We believe that our technique has the potential to improve the precision of static analysis by temporarily deviating from the program's execution order during the analysis phase. The implementation guide also explains how this technique can be easily integrated into existing analysis tools as an extension of the existing analysis. This extension allows the analysis to be applied not only to the main program regions, but also to the interim results derived by the analysis. We are confident that our technique can be a valuable addition to existing analysis methods if properly implemented. Recent advances in recommender systems have propelled them to the forefront of business priorities. Despite the existing reputation systems' effectiveness at identifying trustworthy users, they overlook the broader impact of their users' interactions with the systems. This research introduces Interactive Reputation Systems (IRSs) which go beyond mere trust estimation by incorporating users' interactive behaviors. In our proposed model, an IRS is composed of two main components - a reputation estimator and a interactive updater - which work in tandem to update users' reputations based on their interactions and estimate their trustworthiness. By leveraging an iterative backpropagation framework, our IRS can address the inherent feedback loop and ensure efficient optimization. Experimental results demonstrate the superior performance of our proposed approach over state-of-the-art methods on diverse problem settings. Furthermore, our proposed model enables the development of a visualizer that provides actionable insights for business professionals, enabling them to utilize the proposed IRS in practical scenarios. The implementation of our proposed approach, known as SIFN, is made available under an open-source license. However, the same approach may not be as effective when dealing with code-switched translation tasks, particularly those involving high levels of code-switching. In our research, we employed a thorough methodology to investigate the impact of data augmentation on CSMT. Our contributions include: (i) a comprehensive analysis of the existing word substitution methods and their limitations, (ii) an in-depth examination of the efficacy of parallel and cross-lingual approaches to word substitution in CSMT, and (iii) an investigation of how to adapt these word substitution methods to mitigate the effects of over-correction and improve data augmentation performance. Our experiments on an Arabic-English CSMT dataset showed that (i) data augmentation can be beneficial for CSMT, (ii) parallel approaches outperform cross-lingual methods, and (iii) increasing the lexical similarity between human annotations and artificially generated data can improve CSMT performance. Our findings highlight the importance of careful consideration when employing data augmentation methods in CSMT. We will publicly deposit our code to facilitate reproducibility. In scientific simulation, achieving and preserving a well-posed solution is just the beginning. In the context of solving partial differential equations through multidimensional finite element methods, the goal is to maintain a positive definite solution while dealing with incomplete observations of the solution's state. To this end, we utilize a convex optimization approach to develop a filtering technique that not only calculates a physically valid state but also preserves the underlying problem's structural properties. By formulating an optimization problem that represents the manifold of positive definite matrices, the proposed method ensures that the reconstructed state aligns with the available data and maintains its positive definiteness. To efficiently solve this optimization, we employ a novel, differential manifold-based strategy that incorporates factorization-based methods and is complemented by a robust initialization technique to guarantee a high-quality solution. To evaluate its effectiveness, we implement and test the proposed method in a variety of large-scale simulations and demonstrate its ability to maintain the solution's positive definiteness even under noisy conditions. Furthermore, our results indicate that the proposed method outperforms existing alternatives in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency. To support its practical application, we provide a detailed guide on how to use the proposed method in real-world simulations and make the corresponding Python code available for download. Our study demonstrates that the proposed algorithm's computational runtime scales well with the size of the solution's mesh, making it a valuable tool for researchers and engineers working with complex simulations. In a setting of social transfer learning, agents can draw from previous experiences with other agents who exhibit certain behaviors. However, agents often find themselves in a situation where their actions are met with a response that was not anticipated, due to the inherent unpredictability of the actions of their counterparts. We refer to this aspect as the intrinsic challenge of the context of transfer, specifically regarding how agents adapt to the actions of their counterparts. To address this, we have developed a framework - Transfer Empowerment Framework - aimed at harnessing the value of agents' past experiences in a setting where their actions are met with variable responses. We have demonstrated the effectiveness of this framework in a scenario where two agents engage in a mutual coordination process, specifically an iterated matching pen game, with a focus on evaluating the contribution of our approach beyond state-of-the-art methods and empirical baselines. The reliability of solar wind predictions and their precise calculation are crucial for furthering understanding of the sun's behavior, yet existing low-resolution wind measurements contain systematic errors, hindering predictive accuracy. To determine and correct these errors, a statistical model was developed to estimate wind measurements, but it contains biases that affect its accuracy. To rectify this issue, a method was proposed to correct the model by utilizing high-quality wind data. Specifically, the method involves reversing the bias of the statistical model using corresponding high-quality wind data, then adjusting the model parameters to minimize bias in the training data. This method has shown promising results in reducing bias in the model. Moreover, the bias correction technique was applied to solar radio type III emission data, yielding improved source time profiles with enhanced resolution and reliability. This advancement enables the generation of more accurate and precise solar wind predictions, the demonstration of which is currently hindered by the bias in the statistical model. To produce reliable predictions, a corrective technique similar to the one used for wind data was employed to remove the bias in the emission model. As a result, the source time profiles with bias correction exhibit lower standard deviations, indicating improved predictions. Ultimately, the bias correction technique's effectiveness is measured by its ability to align predicted and observed solar wind parameters across various scales, yielding higher correlation coefficients with correction and demonstrating its potential to refine predictive accuracy. Furthermore, the bias correction technique's applicability and usability are shown through the demonstration of its success in two distinct, empirically driven models for estimating solar radio type III emission data. To achieve this, the method involves reversing the bias of the models by inverting the corresponding cumulative distribution functions, then adjusting the model parameters to minimize bias in the training data. Using these modified models, the technique achieved bias correction in the solar radio type III emission data, resulting in improved predictive accuracy and a more refined understanding of the sun's corona and solar wind characteristics. Notably, the theoretical explanation for the success of the bias correction technique suggests that its application to the solar wind and other phenomena could lead to a significant enhancement in predictive accuracy, ultimately refining our understanding of the sun's behavior. Importantly, the technique's effectiveness is attributed to its ability to account for the bias introduced during the statistical analysis of temporal data, a common challenge in the study of the sun's behavior. This bias, referred to as the reference bias, is a characteristic of all temporal datasets and must be addressed by correcting the model using high-quality data, as demonstrated by the technique's application to solar radio type III emission data.

Von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem determines the convergence rate of the average operator in a finite-dimensional Hilbert space. We investigate and quantify the convergence of spectral measurements, focusing on a basis-related object, under both ergodic and non-ergodic assumptions. Our results reveal that the convergence rate heavily relies on the ergodicity of the system and the choice of basis. In the non-ergodic case, we establish a general method for determining the optimal convergence rate of the average operator when a specific basis is used, based on the spectral properties of the system's matrix. This approach is particularly useful in dealing with systems having a finite number of states. We also provide concrete rate examples for both ergodic and non-ergodic systems. Our work is set in the context of quantum systems, and its implications are discussed from both a theoretical and practical perspective, with support from numerical experiments. Additionally, we derive a condition for the asymptotic independence of measurements performed in different bases. Our results are available in the form of open-source Python code for public use. With respect to related work, our rates are superior to existing rates, particularly for systems equipped with multiple bases. Our study contributes to the development of quantifiable convergence rates in a multi-method approach. To facilitate replication and verification of our findings, the associated code is available at https://github.com/alexkurlan/ergodic-convergence.

We analyzed and forecasted wildfire severity at two locations: outside active wildfires and across entire wildfire seasons, utilizing antecedent precipitation and temperature as predictive factors. We compared the performance of multiple models, including an enhanced Simple Machine Learning algorithm and models based on EPA Burn Pixel and Dynamic Threshold, and our results revealed a new measure of wildfire severity that correlates with atmospheric particulate matter. This paper focuses on simplifying deep neural networks by identifying and eliminating unnecessary parameters. Previous approaches usually minimize overall model complexity. In contrast, we propose a new method that takes into account the significance of individual model parameters in predicting the model's output, measured by their prediction quality scores. We apply an observation-based simplification technique that leverages score distributions to determine which parameters to drop. Unlike existing methods, this approach enables flexible design of the output prediction quality metric. Based on the output score distribution, we define a new metric called output confidence score (OC). We propose an OC-based simplification technique that iteratively prunes parameters based on their removal impact on the score distribution. We evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed method on two datasets: CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, demonstrating that it achieves a substantial reduction in parameters while maintaining or even improving the model's accuracy. Experiment results reveal that our method reduces the number of parameters on ImageNet by 25%, while only suffering from a slight drop in accuracy. We also create a new dataset derived from ImageNet by extracting the features of a mobileNet model, representing a comprehensive and accurately labeled dataset. We compare the proposed method with state-of-the-art parameter optimisation techniques including NASNet, MobileNet and SnaspShot, showing that it outperforms them using the output prediction quality scores as model constraints. As a result, we propose a new method for mobile device applications: AutoScore. Based on novel iterative score distribution pruning technique, AutoScore is independent of the model architecture and can be used as a model-agnostic method for simplifying deep neural networks. We evaluate the method on two datasets: CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, demonstrating that it achieves a reduction in the number of parameters of 78% and still maintains more than 95% of the original accuracy. Furthermore, we compare the proposed method with existing state-of-the-art optimisation techniques including NASNet, MobileNet and SnaspShot, showing that it outperforms them by a large margin on the ImageNet dataset. We also test the generalisation ability of the method by increasing the size of the dataset: after 10 iterations on the larger dataset, the method achieves a reduction in the number of parameters of 85% while maintaining 98% of the original accuracy. We also demonstrate the effectiveness of the method on simplifying a vision transformer model. We evaluate the method on the small ImageNet dataset labelled by around 1.3 million images. We compare the proposed method with state-of-the-art optimisation techniques

We've established two and five measure-based elliptic equations across two and five dimensions, respectively. Our PDEs entail an elliptic operator and a given measure as a fixed element. Notably, these equations exhibit distinctive characteristics when compared to standard elliptic equations, particularly in regards to their being over-determined or under-determined. Consequently, their solution sets exhibit varying degrees of expansibility. Furthermore, a fundamental question arises as to the solvability of these equations under minimal assumptions on the boundary conditions, given that the boundary conditions themselves are constrained by the given measure. Additionally, we've demonstrated the existence and uniqueness of the boundary conditions under optimal conditions, namely when the given measure is supported on a line or a point. Our approach to solving these equations involves a strategy that is both classical and modern, as well as an application of the non-tangential maximum principle under Radon transforms. Our method also allows us to derive new well-posedness results for Calderón-Zygmund operators in weighted Lebesgue spaces, particularly in regards to operators such as the Hardy-Littlewood maximal function and the Hilbert transform, for which we establish standard results across dimensions two and five, respectively. Our findings have been successfully tested on diverse classes of surface measures, including those derived from the Lebesgue integrals on lines and the Fourier transforms of measures on lines. Moreover, our approach is consistent with the known generalities for compact spectral measures, particularly in regards to the eigenfunctions of the given operators. Ultimately, our method allows us to derive a concise expression for the solution of the under-determined measure-based elliptic equations in terms of the given data, thereby facilitating its numerical approximation and visualization. As such, our work has both theoretical and practical implications. Previous research on quantum key distribution often assumed equal randomness for all users, but in practice, we work with non-uniform random seeds. We derive two distinct distance measures: the maximum single-user error and a multi-user error that considers simultaneous eavesdropper attacks. We apply this analysis to two popular privacy amplification functions - the binary additive combiner followed by a CFB counter, and a CFB counter alone - calculating the variation in our distance measures as a function of the counter size. We also compare our results to the information-theoretic capacity of the corresponding combiner, revealing a performance gap that decreases as the counter grows. We then suggest a practical approach to mitigate this gap, demonstrating through simulation that the gap can be nearly eliminated with an appropriate choice of counter size. A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons.
This paper investigates the integration of computational methods for clustering to optimize human labeling efficiency when using comparisons of similar items.
We propose a system known as VACR, which aids in ranking agents based on observed behaviors, thereby reducing the number of required human labels.
Our experiments with two tasks – a multi-objective point positioning task and a complex robotic insertion task – demonstrate VACR's capability to significantly reduce labeling requirements while accurately identifying agents' relative performance levels. As a result, VACR can effectively lower the total human labeling cost by several times.

Recent advancements in dialogue processing have been achieved through the use of large-scale transformer-based models pre-trained on large dialogue corpora.  Although previous methods have relied on heuristically-derived and task-specific representations of semantic meaning, we introduce the FED model, which learns meaning representations through a unified neural framework.  By doing so, FED is able to leverage the benefits of being fine-tuned for downstream dialogue tasks without requiring manually-designed features.  Furthermore, FED is capable of enhancing single-task models, including those using contrasting negative samples, without task-specific hyperparameter tuning.  Experimental results demonstrate that FED achieves state-of-the-art performance in dialogue classification and matching, while also surpassing the performance of the widely-used BERT model, which is available for download on the HF-DIALOG library. To establish trust and ensure fairness, as well as hold developers accountable, it's crucial to assess and evaluate the interpretability of AI models in various applications. Despite numerous proposals, a universally acceptable method for measuring interpretability has yet to be established. In this paper, we propose a new approach to quantitatively assess and compare the interpretability of machine learning models using a cognitive learning model and the Cognitive Complexity Score (CCS). The CCs represents the complexity of cognitive processes involved in learning a particular explanation, and its primary metric is the number of hypotheses generated during the learning process. By assigning a weight to each hypothesis based on its contribution to model accuracy, the CCs increases as the accuracy decreases, indicating a clearer understanding of the model's inner workings. We apply this measure to several datasets, including UDA scenarios, and demonstrate its effectiveness in evaluating and comparing the interpretability of traditional and more advanced machine learning models, including ensemble methods, as well as LIME and SHAP explainers. Additionally, we propose two strategies for enhancing the CCs: increasing the weight of hypotheses related to specific feature values to highlight their importance, and adjusting the learning rate to prevent over-fitting or under-fitting by stopping the learning process before the model achieves full accuracy. We also provide access to our source code on GitHub at https://github.com/scarpa81/cognitive_interpretability. The numerical results and plots are available at the URL https://github.com/scarpa81/cognitive_interpretability/results. Furthermore, we note that our approach, unlike other methods, does not rely on either human annotations or human-derived constructs like class names and attributes. We also emphasize that explanations, including those generated in this study, are intended for human consumption and should not be viewed as explanations of the model itself but rather as auxiliary tools to help humans understand the model. We also provide three possible uses of the CCs: as a tool for developers to assess and improve their models, as a mechanism for measuring the interpretability of third-party models for companies providing AI services, and as a means to estimate the consumption effort required for creating explanations in just-in-time scenarios. Ultimately, the CCs can serve as a versatile tool for various applications, with an example of its effectiveness in enhancing just-in-time explainability through a simple interaction with users being presented in the paper.
