A typical strategy for modeling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a nonhomogeneous Poisson process. While this method has the advantage of efficient Bayesian inference, it is hampered by the Poisson process's time transformation issue, which causes posterior concentrations into unrealistic regions. We show that threshold-dependent ancillary parameters' Markov chain components consisting of two independent components under Bayesian sampling often fall into these unrealistic regions. We propose a new parameterization scheme in a way that keeps the posterior distribution unchanged and ensure the resulting components of the Markov chain have nonnegative values. We discuss how this new scheme affects Bayesian sampling and model comparison. We provide theoretical analysis for this new scheme based on the geometric dissection of the parameter space and numerical evidence for its improvement over the original scheme based on extreme-value properties. Our research focuses on extreme events such as rainfall, wind speed, and floodings in the city of Zurich. Our results indicate that the proposed new parameterization scheme results in efficient convergence of the Markov chain. Therefore, accurate Bayesian inference and model comparison can be performed for extreme events. Our research relies heavily on numerical methods and visualizations to analyze how the Poisson process works. Our article includes supplementary material, including related papers, data, and additional figures. The COMET framework, aimed at enhancing AI capabilities with common sense knowledge, is the focal point of this workshop.  A new commonplace graph, COMET-ATOMIC 2020, is introduced, which expands upon its predecessor by encompassing 133 relations found in extensive datasets and thereby enlarging the common sense knowledge base that AI systems can tap into.  This paper outlines COMET-ATOMIC 2020's development and showcases its utility through two novel applications: answering complex questions with multiple parts and filling in missing information in text.  By making the graph and corresponding ATOMIC 2020 relations set available, COMET-ATOMIC 2020 offers ample opportunities for training, testing, and evaluating AI models seeking to harness common sense knowledge.  A new benchmark for neural network architectures, based on these relationships, could potentially lead to breakthroughs in understanding and utilizing common sense knowledge.  This event marks the third iteration of the COMET-ATOMIC series and the first COMET-ATOMIC 2020 workshop, which brought together leading researchers and data creators to discuss and share knowledge on symbolic and neural commonplace graph topics.  A new version of the COMET-ATOMIC 2020 dataset, incorporating annotations for non-English languages, is being made available to the public, accompanied by a related paper titled "COMET-ATOMIC 2020: Multilingual Expansion of a Large-Scale Question Answering Dataset for Grounding Language in Common Sense Knowledge".  Additionally, a related video titled "COMET-ATOMIC 2020: Multilingual Expansion" can be found at https://youtu.be/Ni8jY3xk8gE.  This event was a component of the 2020 Association for the Advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AAAI) Conference on Artificial Intelligence.  A related document, describing the COMET-ATOMIC 2020 dataset and benchmark, is being made available at https://github.com/comet-ontology/comet-atomic-2020.  A related GitHub project, allowing for training, testing, and evaluation of the COMET-ATOMIC 2020 dataset and benchmark, is being hosted at https://github.com/comet-ontology/comet-atomic-2020-benchmark. We detail the pipeline utilized for the Hi-GAL survey's data compression, which utilized the HI-Green-Bank Survey's 21 cm line spectral data to produce 34 frequency channels for each of the 41 x 41 square degree fields, with an effective 1.5 arcmin beam size. We outline the pipeline's individual stages: initial calibration, models of dust emission and CO emission, the reanalysis of spectral data, and the application of a mask to conceal bright sources. We also provide an update on the survey, previously delayed due to technical issues, with fields completely collected and scheduled for observation over the next two years. Future developments are expected to expand the survey to at least 200 fields, with the goal of observing the Milky Way's galactic disc through a combination of the Hi-GAL survey's dust emission and the Planck satellite's 353 GHz foreground maps. We present initial results from simulated data, with the goal of assessing the effectiveness of this approach using the, currently operational, Green Bank Observatory's 21 cm line receiver. We also present a concept for a more efficient compression technique that could be implemented in real-time during observations. This would require the development of a, previously conceived, real-time data processing system for the Green Bank Observatory's 21 cm line receiver, with the ability to simultaneously observe and process up to 200 fields. We also provide an update on the presence of 12CO and 13CO background interference in the Hi-GAL survey's data, with the goal of assessing its potential impact on the survey's data compression pipeline. We also provide a conceptual framework for implementing the data compression pipeline in the Green Bank Observatory's 30m telescope during observations, with the ability to simultaneously observe and process up to 200 fields. This would utilize a, previously developed, real-time data processing system for the Green Bank Observatory's 21 cm line receiver, with the ability to generate up to 34 frequency channels for each of the 41 x 41 square degree fields, with the effective 1.5 arcmin beam size. The formation of the first stars in a galaxy depends on the characteristics of its initial metal content, with supernovae contributing to the diversity through the release of varying amounts of elements. However, the extent to which pre-existing metals in the interstellar space affected the initial star formation remains a topic of ongoing research. In this study, we examine two populations of metal-rich, generation-one stars in the globular cluster NGC 2808 and determine a standard metal content range of $-0.73 < [Fe/H] < -0.63$ with a margin of error of 0.09 dex. In addition, we found a slight but not significant variation in the abundance of alpha elements within this range, which further indicates that generation-one stars within this cluster have a relatively standard metal content. These results are based on a detailed re-evaluation of existing spectroscopic data. A small number of stellar members in this study were identified through the analysis of their iron abundance across 23 different papers. If the iron abundance measurements, which have a diverse methodological composition, are correct, it implies that generation-one stars within this galaxy have a relatively standard metal content. In addition, we found no evidence of a distinct spectral characteristic, which would suggest the presence of hotter stars and thus indicate that a relatively cool and metal-rich globular cluster is not generating the diversity observed in its metal content. In addition to this, we found no evidence of a pre-galactic spread in the iron abundance found within this galaxy through the analysis of its alpha element abundance. A detailed analysis and discussion of these findings are included in this study. 

The study involved a re-evaluation of existing data from various sources including: 

1. A catalogue of iron abundance measurements for stars within NGC 2808, which was initially presented in Giannetti et al. 2014.
2. Detailed spectroscopic data for five stars within this galaxy, which was initially presented in Wan et al. 2017.
3. Derived values of the iron and alpha element abundances for these five stars, which was initially presented in Marotti de Sciarra et al. 2015.
4. Derived values of various stellar characteristics for two evolutionary models with different iron content levels, which was initially presented in Sanna et al. 2012.

These data were initially presented in respective studies, which were in turn based on analysis of:

* Giannetti et al. (2014) 
* Wan et al. (2017)
* Marotti de Sciarra

Interestingly, quantum theories based on physical measurements exhibit predictable patterns when applying frequentist statistics. It has been claimed that this consistency stems from Bayesian update rules being inherently sound. We, however, argue that this consistency can be understood as arising from a more fundamental level - that of the mathematical properties of quantum theories. We demonstrate that the patterns in measurement predictions emerge as a natural consequence of the underlying quantum framework. This outcome suggests that the patterns may remain intact even if a non-Bayesian approach to inference is adopted. In a related development, proposed solutions to the measurement problem often focus on resolving the long-standing shift between base states and observables. When t equals 2, the only non-trivial element in H(t, k) has order 2 to the power of k+1. This result reinforces a previous finding established by H. Adams. The reason behind our analysis's success lies in the ability to utilize a combination of techniques, including the methods of Dold and Grysinski as well as the methods of Mike Shulman's article on stable homotopy categories without axioms. Our analysis suggests that for any given value of t, the ring structure of H(t, k) is highly constrained, consisting of either a trivial ring or a ring with a single non-trivial element of order 2. Harper's article to establish a relationship between the algebraic structure of the group H(t, k) and the algebraic structure of the group D(t, k) consisting of functions from the integers to the integers that satisfy a specific relation. Recent advancements in visual learning have led to the development of multiple large-scale image databases catering to diverse end-to-end machine learning applications such as object detection and segmentation. These databases primarily focus on still images, despite being indexed using static metadata like image file names and have not yet adapted to incorporate temporal information. This paper introduces a dynamic indexing approach for large image databases that integrates temporal frame metadata. The proposed method allows for the creation of multi-layered hierarchical structures that can be tailored to various query types including rapid object detection, scene propagation, and image retrieval. The effectiveness of dynamic indexing is demonstrated through a prototype web-based browser application for searching video databases, showcasing seamless interaction and fast retrieval of visual content. The introduced technique is compatible with existing static indexing schemes, making it an ideal solution for incorporating temporal information in still image databases. The created video database, Dynamic Yale, is introduced as a test case for evaluating dynamic indexing efficiency. Indexing speed and query retrieval times are analyzed and tested, along with temporal metadata integration efficiency assessments via tree height analysis. The research presents a method for dynamic image indexing that can revolutionize browser interactions with video databases, providing a platform for end-to-end machine learning queries. Physical layer keyless authentication (PLKA) involves authenticating a user
or device at the physical layer of a communication system without utilizing
encryption or secret information being shared with that user or device.
Authentication in the physical layer is typically carried out using genuine or
adversarial channels to verify communication links. We explore PLKA in a
additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel and compare it to the traditional
cryptographic method. Our solution to AWGN PLKA involves framing authentication
as a decision problem based on received signal strength, for which we provide
accurate probability metrics and an efficient verification technique. Our tests
show that the AWGN PLKA verification technique offers 99% accuracy when the signal
to noise ratio is 20, a level significantly higher than that achieved by the
binary relative strength of signal technique which achieves only around 68% at the
same SNR value, with further improvements in accuracy expected at higher SNR
values. We also discuss how AWGN PLKA can be applied to wireless networks. Our
tests using wireless networks show that the AWGN PLKA verification technique
performed consistently better than the binary strength of signal technique. Our
work at the physical layer has led to the development of a security interface
splitting framework, a concept in which the interface is divided into two parts
one of which is applied at the physical layer and the other at a higher level of
communication protocol. Our splitting framework provides a balanced approach to
achieving security and non-repudiation while minimizing interference to existing
communication interfaces. We outline a possible split of the interface into two
parts at the physical layer and the higher levels of communication protocol. Our
tests show that the interface splitting framework performed consistently better at
the physical layer than the binary strength of signal technique. Our work has a
number of potential applications, including the authentication of IoT devices.

Long-term particle trajectories on corrugated, infinite washboard surfaces exhibit recurring patterns of lateral shifts and stationary advances. Average displacement over extended periods approximates a linear function of time. Nonetheless, individual trajectories lack determinable average velocities due to the intertwined nature of both stationary and transverse motion. We develop a method to decompose and separately analyze both types of motion, thereby revealing a particle's predictable, linear motion in a particular direction. This motion is unaffected by perpendicular fluctuations. A key condition allows these perpendicular fluctuations to be a stationary random process. Our research provides a general approach to understanding the long-term behavior of particles moving under conservative forces with periodic and stochastically perturbed dynamics. We illustrate the applicability of our methods by examining both the Arrhenius law's physical basis and the established results on long-term dispersionless behavior. We further demonstrate this approach through the numerical simulation of a two-dimensional model of a Fenton reaction. The fundamental principles we derive are straightforward and can be seen in the long-term behavior of underdamped particles on a one-dimensional washboard surface with both deterministic and white noise perturbations. The autocorrelation of perpendicular fluctuations determines the predictable, linear perpendicular velocity. This is the expected, deterministic behavior. In graph theory, an upward planar drawing is a two-dimensional visual representation where all edges are drawn as straight lines without intersecting one another. This type of drawing is equivalent to a specific type of order-preserving function called a labeling. Upward planarity has numerous applications across various fields, including computational biology, the analysis of financial data, and multimedia documentation. Due to its intricate nature, it has been challenging to determine whether a given graph is upward-planar using traditional methods, but in recent years, researchers have developed faster algorithms using parameterized techniques. Building on previous work by Hahn and Wanke, who developed a parameterized algorithm in 2010, we provide a new parameterized solution to the upward planarity problem, utilizing a specific graph structure called a 5-leaf-labeled graph. This new technique has a run time of O(n^6) and can be executed through a series of linear equations representing the specific order-preserving structure of the graph. Additionally, we employ the concept of crossing number as an alternate condition for determining upward planarity in graphs lacking a specific cycle, referred to as K4-minus. The crossing number condition allows us to establish a specific threshold for determining whether a K4-minus graph is upward-planar or not. Specifically, we demonstrate that any parameterized solution to the problem must have a run time of at least 3^t * n, where t is the size of the symmetric group and n is the number of vertices in the graph. Crowdsourced image datasets, often marred by noise, pose a significant challenge for even the most sophisticated neural networks. This difficulty arises from class imbalance and ambiguous image classifications that require consideration of uncertainty. This study proposes a method to address these issues by leveraging ensemble modeling, a statistical representation of uncertainty, and an information-theoretic approach to quantify dataset quality and identify noisy examples. Ensemble modeling aggregates models with varying architectures, effectively counteracting overconfident predictions resulting from noisy labels. 'Human softmax' distributions evaluate model confidence in classifications, while entropic measures assess uncertainty and dataset reliability across classes. This method is applied to the CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 datasets, providing insight into dataset and model uncertainty. Experimental results demonstrate that ensemble modeling, soft uncertainty distributions, and entropic uncertainty metrics can improve model performance and identify noisy examples. Furthermore, this approach allows for the evaluation of dataset quality and the assessment of models relative to state-of-the-art image classification models. Despite being trained on visually balanced datasets, models perform better on imbalanced crowdsourced datasets, highlighting the advantages of ensemble modeling and uncertainty-based metrics for addressing noise in such datasets. To accomplish this, we examine the reverse process of $W W$ production, measuring it via an exclusive four jet final state to establish a relationship between the observed W boson mass and its coupling to the Higgs field.  It's discovered that the required effective parameter space is consistent with existing constraints from the CMS and ATLAS at the 95% confidence level.  Notably, this finding implies that the type-X 2HDM model is a feasible option to explain both the W boson and muon anomalies.  Further research suggests that future Muon ($g-2$) measurements could reduce the needed parameter space even further.  Lastly, this type-X 2HDM model creates an opportunity to observe and study the decay of the lighter Higgs, potentially yielding valuable insights into this process at the 14 TeV LHC.  To this end, suggested analysis recommendations for the CMS and ATLAS are offered for validating these predictions and confirming the type-X 2HDM model.  Moreover, it's expected that future Muon ($g-2$) measurements and the 30-100 TeV muon collider can further confirm the validity of this model at the quantum level in the future.  Specifically, it's anticipated that the Muon collider may be able to detect the presence of this type-X 2HDM model up to a scale larger than 10 TeV.  To sum up, the type-X 2HDM model represents an important and significant option for explaining both the W boson and muon anomalies, and it will likely be testable and confirmable using various future muon colliders and lepton colliders that are currently under consideration.  Specifically, it's predicted that the FCC-muon collider may be able to discover this type-X 2HDM model at odds with the standard model at the 5 sigma level, should it operate at 100 TeV. Notably, our method does not rely on third-party data and our approach to pseudo-label creation is novel in this field. This study examines multi-stage games where players have limited information and focuses on the cognitive abilities of these games' solutions. We propose a hierarchical learning method of sufficient cognition and show that this approach can identify solutions with the lowest required cognitive level. Furthermore, we introduce a metric to measure the minimum necessary cognition and investigate its properties. Our work also includes a numerical example illustrating the effectiveness of our proposed method. Interestingly, this study reveals that the required cognition for solving these games is directly related to the number of stages. Moreover, we demonstrate that introducing cognition into lower levels of a hierarchical framework does not affect solutions at higher levels, as long as cognition is implemented at or below the lowest underlying layer. This counterintuitive result is consistent with a manager having complete knowledge but individual employees being unaware of the situation. Our mathematical results are substantiated by a numerical example. Finally, this study considers the issue of robustness in games with limited information and uncertain cognition levels. We propose a solution concept that incorporates both cognitive abilities and data uncertainty. Our numerical example demonstrates that the required cognition under uncertainty is greater than in situations with certain cognition levels. Moreover, the required cognition under uncertainty grows rapidly with the size of the problem, as illustrated in our numerical example. In terms of methodological contributions, this study introduces a general approach for evaluating the required cognition of solutions in linear decision-making systems with limited information and uncertain cognition levels. Our work is represented by a vector formulation that expands on the existing exponential loss formulation. This transformation identifies solutions with the lowest required cognition under data uncertainty for any linear decision-making system. Our time and computational complexity results for identifying these solutions are presented in a mathematical format. Our work is demonstrated through a series of examples and numerical experiments. The approaches proposed in this study have been successfully tested and shown to be practical and efficient in a real-world economic context, with our recent application to data from the US Department of Transportation. Each decade, the global population grows by approximately 3 billion, resulting in an average increase of 380 million per year. A notable increase in population occurs in Africa, with its population expected to triple by 2100. In Mozambique, the population is projected to double over the same period, resulting in significant challenges if urban infrastructure development is to be maintained. The country's population data, necessary for informing development policies and strategies, is currently estimated using a combination of censuses and a simple linear growth model. However, this approach poses challenges, particularly during the decade-leading up to a national census, when it relies on a 5- to 16-year-old population growth rate. The replacement of the linear growth model with a probabilistic framework, based on the population's skew distribution, yields a more accurate and reliable population estimation method. We propose and compare two estimation methods: one that involves fitting a Skew Normal distribution to the same single piece of information used by the linear model, and another based on combining two previous national census decade estimates, using a weighted average of SN population growth rate estimates. The new methodologies exhibit lower estimation errors for the Mozambique population. Specifically, estimating a single census decade as required for the initial 14 years following a national census is more accurate than the linear growth model with an average error reduction of 66%. Additionally, our results indicate that incorporating data from two previous census decades as required for the 5- to 16-year-old age group, yields a significant error decrease of about 70% when compared to the linear growth model. The replacement of the linear growth model with these new estimation methods can contribute to a more sustainable population estimation process in Mozambique. Furthermore, our study highlights the general advantages of using the SN distribution for population growth estimation, resulting in lower estimation errors for both single and multiple census decade estimates. The method of combining estimates involves a simple weighted average of SN population growth rate estimates from two previous census decades. To accomplish this, we propose the Hopper model, built around a multi-hop transformer architecture that enables efficient spatiotemporal inference. These findings provide valuable insights for remote robot control designers and practitioners, emphasizing the need to invest in interactive QoE assessment tools. The study used a mixed-effects regression model to analyze the data, which showed a statistically significant positive correlation between the quality of the experience and users' emotional states. The study highlighted two key aspects: first, the emotional states were influenced by the combination of an experience factor and specific impairment factors, which provided fresh insights for design improvement; second, the results provided new perspectives on the characteristics of users' emotional states in response to various impairments during remote operations. This research develops a novel fuzzy k-means approach to cluster high-dimensional data across multiple subspaces. The algorithm is specifically designed for high-dimensional data sets where features can vary in relevance and importance, affecting the quality of the cluster. To overcome this limitation, our method modifies the traditional fuzzy k-means objective function using two key components. First, the entropy of cluster membership probabilities is maximized to ensure uniform cluster sizes. Second, the within-cluster covariance distances replace the traditional squared distance between points, allowing features to be weighted based on their individual variances. The algorithm, dubbed EKMC, is empirically validated using 14 datasets that exhibit varying levels of heteroscedasticity and uneven feature variances. Our experimental findings demonstrate that EKMC outperforms its counterparts in terms of accurate cluster recovery, achieving success rates of up to 100%. Additionally, our method converges quickly with only a minimal number of iterations (usually 20-30), requiring competitive computational resources compared to established algorithms. Notably, our method's performance surpasses the recent state-of-the-art approach, the Entropy-based Re-weighted Fuzzy k-Means algorithm. The proposed EKMC method is expected to contribute significantly to the clustering of high-dimensional data characterized by varying features, uneven feature variances, and within-cluster covariance distances. The associated implementation can be found on GitHub under https://github.com/MathMaRi/Variable-Feature-Weighted-Fuzzy-k-Means. Mixtures of experts, a type of Gaussian mixture model, have been challenging to fit directly. Instead, iterative algorithms recursively assign data points to expert distributions, which are fitted separately parameters. Yet, conventional algorithms struggle to recover the expert parameters, leading to suboptimal performance and instabilities in practice. To address this issue, we develop a straightforward, direct method for fitting such mixtures, by first determining the assignment of data points under the assumption of expert distributions. Our algorithm then uses the data points assigned to each expert to fit a separate Gaussian distribution. Our approach overcomes the limitations of existing algorithms by providing a guaranteed solution and improving convergence, while also matching state-of-the-art performance and offering a competitive runtime. Additionally, we extend this method to handle missing data using the EM algorithm and apply it to real-world data analysis. Comparing our approach with other existing algorithms shows its superiority in terms of recovery accuracy, convergence, and computational efficiency. Lastly, we highlight the benefits of using our algorithm to improve the performance of Mixtures of Experts-based neural networks. [Abstract]

Researchers have successfully observed for the first time the transfer of transverse and longitudinal beam emittances between two beams using the CEA-DSM's LNF beam line in France. The experiment involved directing a 590 MeV/c linear electron beam at a stationary target, which then interacted with a 25 mA/c ammonia beam. The resulting captured electron bunch, having undergone both transverse and longitudinal momentum transfer, was detected with a high-resolution screen and a nanosecond-resolution pulse generator, revealing detailed information about the bunch's initial and final temporal and spatial profiles. By analyzing these profiles, scientists were able to calculate both the average and average-squared values of the transverse and longitudinal beam emittances before and after the interaction, thereby quantitatively assessing the transferred emittances. According to their measurements, approximately 75% of the transverse emittance and 83% of the longitudinal emittances were found to have been transferred in the interaction. The observed values of the transferred emittances compare favorably with the results of a self-similarity-based model, which predicted that about 80% of both transverse and longitudinal emittances would be transferred in the interaction. The agreement between the measured results and the model prediction confirms the hypothesis of emittance transfer in the collision between the fast and slow beams. The capabilities of this method for manipulating and measuring emittances were also explored. The researchers proposed its application in the formation of low-enstrophy, high-spatial coherence electron bunches via a multi-stage gas-filled linac and in the production of free-electron laser pulses with extremely high peak powers. The observed emittance transfer between the fast and slow beams could potentially be used as a means of emittance compensation in particle accelerators, which could lead to a significant reduction in the length required for a linear collider to reach the same level of luminosity as the current circular colliders. The existing beam delivery systems at radiofrequency linear accelerators, such as the Fermilab LINAC and the Paul Scherrer Institute LINAC, could be easily modified with the addition of a gas-filled linac at one end to achieve this goal. The proposed system would allow for a simplified design with no need for complicated electron beam manipulation systems, such as laser photoinization or radiofrequency deflection, to create the low-enstrophy electron bunches needed for a free-electron laser pulse. Although social interaction models like Social Force have comprehensive memory, their limitations in handling sudden events like collisions or changes in pace make integrating short-term predictions challenging. To bridge this gap, a new approach is proposed that combines the benefits of sequence modeling and social awareness for more accurate predictions. Specifically, a fully social-aware predictor is developed, its performance benchmarked against ground truth, and its practical applicability demonstrated through comparison with state-of-the-art methods on multiple datasets. Furthermore, this approach is used to create a safety-aware navigation system, demonstrating its effectiveness in helping robots avoid collisions. Overall, this work highlights the importance of incorporating past information and social awareness for effective prediction and safe navigation. In the analysis of microscopic image data, experts rely on manual counting and
identification of cells. This process is time-consuming, prone to error, and unsuitable
for numerous specimens. Recently, neural network-based techniques have shown great
promise in automatically classifying cell types based on micrograph images. 
Unfortunately, these models are often highly specialized and only work effectively 
for a particular type of cell. This means that if a user wants to classify another type 
of cell, they would need to train and maintain their own model, which is complicated 
and requires significant technical expertise. To address this, we developed a method 
that combines cell classification models into a single, unified system, enabling it to 
accommodate a wider range of cells with reduced error rates and improved 
overall performance. 
Our technique has been successfully tested on a vast collection of images depicting 
different human white blood cells, and the results show that the integrated model is 
more accurate and efficient than individual models designed for specific cell types. 
This breakthrough has the potential to accelerate and simplify high-throughput analysis 
in various applications, including clinical diagnostics. 
Our integrated model, along with the accompanying code and dataset used in our 
study (e.g. the Anatext dataset and neural network code), are publicly accessible at 
https://github.com/llumanti/BloodCellNet.

The exponential function has the following property when expressed as a Taylor series: 
The partial sum of the series's terms, given by $f^{(n)}\left(x\right)$ with $x$ being any real number and $n$ being a non-negative integer, equals the exponential function itself evaluated at $x$, which is denoted as $\exp\left(x\right)$. 
This means the exponential function can be expressed as a finite series of its own Taylor terms, making the original infinite series an adequate expansion of the exponential function. 
This discovery allows the original infinite exponential series $\exp\left(x\right)$ to be considered an unsatisfactory representation of the exponential function and encourages the use of a higher-order Taylor series that can accurately represent $\exp\left(x\right)\cdot e^{2\pi i k/x}$. 
This improvement in the exponential series leads to the following computational benefits: 
First, the computational effort to calculate the exponential series is reduced because only the first $n$ terms of the series are needed. 
Second, the computational effort to evaluate the exponential series is also reduced because only one $n$-fold iteration of the recursive function $f$ is needed and the base case is easily solved using the identity $\exp\left(x\right)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^{k}}{k!}$. 
This new approach to the exponential series was successfully tested on the eigenvalues of the Cremona transformation, the period of the modular $j$ function, and the zeros of the Riemann zeta function. 
All calculations using the new series were faster by at least a a a factor of $n$ and were often many orders of magnitude faster.

To translate ASR output into written text, inverse text normalization (ITN) is a crucial step, yet numerous language and structure complexities make modern ITN models struggle to achieve high accuracy across various domains. The existing ITN models are limited by their primary reliance on supervised learning and the quality of training data, which can be costly to improve. In response, we have developed data augmentation methods for ITN, aiming to increase its coverage without expanding the training data. Specifically, our techniques aim to boost ITN performance for characteristics like decimal formatting, combined numbers, and compound words. By combining these methods with the most advanced ITN models, we have achieved significant accuracy improvements, with ITN accuracy enhanced by 9.78% for the convolutional model, 11.21% for the transformer model, and 12.06% for the fusion model, with the accuracy measurements being the char-level edit distance, the sentence-level Levenshtein distance, and the char-level Levenshtein distance, respectively. Our current research involves the development of a method to incorporate dynamic and varied personality traits in synthetic speech. We show through studies involving human listeners that the Stochastic Actor-based Personality model is effective in simulating an speaker's personality, and that incorporating personality variability in speech readings makes them sound more natural. We also found that the perceived personality traits of human speakers are shifted in response to high levels of emotional expression. In addition, we present a new approach to simulate social speech traits, known as speech style, and an method to incorporate this attribute in synthetic speech. We have created a dataset of speeches featuring distinct speakers with distinct levels of personality, speech styles, and emotional expression levels. This dataset, known as SpeechStyle2, allows for comprehensive evaluation of speech generation techniques that take into account varied speaker personality. We have used a speech generation pipeline based on the state-of-the-art WaveNet model to create a method for simulating speech that incorporates the Stochastic Actor-based Personality model, and have performed an extensive evaluation of the precision of our model in simulating speaker personality, speech styles, and emotional expression levels. Our results indicate that the Stochastic Actor-based Personality model is highly effective in simulating speaker personality and speech styles. We have also shown that the emotional expression levels of a speaker can significantly impact the perceived personality traits of human speakers. We have also conducted an evaluation of the precision of our model in simulating speaker personality, speech styles, and emotional expression levels. We have also used SpeechStyle2 and learned representations of speech styles to generate synthetic speeches featuring varied personality traits, speech styles, and emotional expression levels. We have also conducted a major evaluation of the synthetic speeches generated by our model and compared them to speeches read by human speakers with distinct personality traits, speech styles, and emotional expression levels. The results of this evaluation show that the model is highly effective in simulating speaker personality, speech styles, and emotional expression levels, and that the synthetic speeches generated by our model sound similar to speeches read by human speakers with distinct personality traits, speech styles, and emotional expression levels. Change detection in remote sensing imagery is an important issue that has been studied extensively. Research has progressed from traditional spectral-based methods to more recent spatio-temporal approaches. This paper focuses on change detection in multiple frames using both spectral and spatial image data. A novel, deep learning-based method, named Feature fusion-DCNN $\triangledown$ (FF-DCNN $\triangledown$), is proposed to identify changes within areas with mixed pixel contents. This approach combines features from spatial and spectral contexts, utilizing a context sharing mechanism to facilitate information exchange. FF-DCNN $\triangledown$ has several adjustable modules, allowing it to achieve high accuracy in detecting changes. This method was tested using two datasets from the SpecTreo1 and TLS Spectroscopy cameras, both of which capture multiple frame images under diverse conditions. Notably, FF-DCNN $\triangledown$ outperformed existing supervised methods while requiring fewer training parameters. Furthermore, the proposed non-linear DCNN $\triangledown$-Net can perform change detection without the need for detailed label information, resulting in accurate pixel classification and robust area of interest detection under various conditions. A comparative study demonstrated that FF-DCNN $\triangledown$ obtains better results than many existing deep learning-based methods, while DCNN $\triangledown$-Net outperforms them by achieving higher overall accuracies, reduced storage needs, and lower computational complexity. This research demonstrates the potential of combining multiple module architectures to address the change detection problem, and also proposes two novel and efficient deep learning-based methods that require minimal resources while achieving high-accuracy results. These techniques have promising applications in multiple fields such as hyperspectral imaging, balloon-based astronomy, and medical research involving tissue analysis. The proposed methods have also been successfully tested across different programming platforms including MATLAB, PyTorch, and CUDA. This study provides a detailed investigation of the change detection problem, along with the mathematical derivation of the DCNN $\triangledown$-Net architecture. As such, it may be of interest to a wide range of researchers working in machine learning, remote sensing, and related fields. Furthermore, the corresponding source code for the FF-DCNN $\triangledown$ and FF-DCNN $\triangledown$-Net methods can be obtained from https://github.comilde1/FF-DCNN$\triangledown$-Net. This code enables the reproduction of the research outcomes and showcases the influence of various parameters and hyper-parameters on the performance of the FF-DCNN

A comprehensive study examines the relationship between residual entropy and viscosity using reference interaction site model (RISM) theory, applied to various molecules and potential models. The results obtained from combining RISM with the Weidlich-Ehrenfest equation for pure components match experimental data on liquid viscosities closely. Considering the complexity of molecular liquids, the proposed correlation between entropy and viscosity is noteworthy. It is also demonstrated that an improved RISM approach, along with composite correlation functions from high-temperature cluster expansions, enables predictions of viscosity that align well with experimental data in 20 different molecular liquids without any additional adjustment to the model parameters. Generally, the models show a moderate to strong correlation with reference to mean absolute error (MAE), with some liquids having MAE values between 10% and 30% and others between 5% and 15%. It is anticipated that the established connection between residual entropy and viscosity can be extended to other properties of molecular liquids through multi-point correlations and optimal model parameter calibration. Moreover, the proposed framework of composite correlation functions is expected to be useful in developing frameworks that can simultaneously model the solvent and mixture properties. The framework of composite correlation functions is based on perturbation theory and corresponds to high-temperature cluster expansions, offering multiple benefits, such as enhanced efficiency, stability, and flexibility. Specifically, it allows for the calculation of multi-body correlation functions and the construction of composite correlation functions from any molecular reference potential, which in turn enables the determination of viscosity and other anisotropic properties. In addition to its use in predicting properties, the proposed framework of composite correlation functions is expected to be a valuable diagnostic tool to analyze the structure of molecular liquids in terms of pair and higher-order correlations and to identify the relevant clusters in potential models and real molecules. In particular, the results obtained from high-temperature cluster expansions indicate a very good agreement between the predicted structure and MAE values, with some liquids having MAE values between 5% and 15% and others between 10% and 30%. The effectiveness of the proposed framework of composite correlation functions and its potential applications to various fields are expected to be significant. The cycle cosmology theory suggests that our universe has gone through alternating periods of expansion and contraction. Specifically, during an expansion phase, gravity's influence diminishes, giving rise to a complex universe with intricate structures. In contrast, during a contraction phase, gravitational force increases, resulting in a simpler, uniformly distributed universe. Since the last expansion, there has been an exponential increase in the rate at which new matter and energy emerge, while the rate of contraction has been steadily increasing due to an exotic dark energy component. Consequently, the contraction phase is now accelerating and will soon be irreversible. A massive planet with similar properties to Earth has been proposed as a potential shelter for life. This hypothetical planet, located in a distant star system, still supports life and might offer a refuge in the distant future. Details about the emergence of dark matter and dark energy are also provided, as well as evidence supporting the theory's validity based on observations of the cosmic microwave background, supernovae, and Baryon Acoustic Oscillations. Furthermore, the theory's mathematical formulation has been broadened to include various assumptions and inferences regarding the birth and death of our universe. One of the notable inferences is that the universe had a beginning but will not have an end, giving rise to the concept of a "cosmic nest." In various safety-critical systems, like aerospace and automotive technology, missed hard deadlines can lead to severe consequences, even fatalities. The advent of Functional Safety standards ISO 26262 and IEC 61508 have made it mandatory for these systems to ensure safe operation by limiting fault probability. To achieve this, developers use safety-related systems, and the resilience of the embedded operating system is taken into consideration while creating safety-related applications. The operating system's functionality is restricted to meet ISO 26262 and IEC 61508's requirements, but this control is lost when the operating system runs on a processor without a separate memory area for its execution. To address this limitation, we have developed T-Visor, a hypervisor for real-time operating systems. By introducing virtualization on real-time operating systems, T-Visor enables partitioning of processor resources, thus allowing a single hypervisor to manage multiple operating systems safely and independently. This partitioning of resources also contributes to enhancing the security of the embedded system. The objective is to develop a computational framework for reconstructing seamless panoramic data from multiple image sequences captured using different camera orientations. Existing algorithms often employ feature-based localization and matching techniques, after which a constant-scale warper is utilized to join the images. However, when capturing sequences with significant differences in camera orientations, the resulting panoramic images may exhibit distorted scales, rendering them incompatible for seamless joining. Existing solutions typically rely on manual adjustment or utilize feature-based localization techniques that are time-consuming and less accurate. In contrast, we introduce a novel approach based on adaptive warpers that facilitate seamless joining of images even when captured with varying camera orientations without the need for explicit feature localization. Our adaptive warpers optimize image seams to minimize distortions, focusing on prior representations of gravity and image characteristics. In instances where images are captured in sequences with known or unknown roll angles, we develop an efficient method for adaptive seam optimization to produce high-quality, geometrically accurate panoramas with natural-looking detail transitions. The proposed framework is validated through comprehensive quantitative and qualitative analyses, demonstrating superior performance in comparison to existing constantscale joiners. Notably, our approach enables the construction of high-resolution panoramic images from image sequences with substantial camera orientation differences, previously considered infeasible with existing methods. Additionally, our adaptation of warpers allows us to join large-scale 360-degree images and videos with minimal online processing requirements, opening up new possibilities for real-time, offline deployment. The accompanying code and pre-trained models are publicly available on the https://github.com/aiharbor/AdaptiveWarper repository. With further advancements, our adaptive seam optimizer may also find applications in other domain-specific joining tasks beyond panoramic reconstruction. Current ensemble based methods in continual learning have limitations.
Firstly, they require offline labeling which is costly.
Secondly, even if task orders are known in advance, acquiring labels is still costly due to the need for annotating all tasks multiple times.
To address these issues, this paper introduces an innovative online continual learning approach where new tasks are continuously added without requiring additional labeling.
To prevent class confusion, this method relies on temporary task grouping rather than permanent tasks, using an ensemble of neural networks to store learned knowledge.
To achieve this, new tasks are first processed individually, while existing tasks with similar data are grouped for consistent class labeling, ensuring that classes learned from one group are not overwritten by other groups.
To ensure online continuity, this method employs an adaptive scheduling system to balance the flow of new tasks with existing groups.
Additionally, to prevent interference when new tasks are added, neural ensemble parameters are separated into two distinct parameters and older groups are gradually transferred to the ensemble as stability is assumed to increase over time.
The method's efficiency in inter-task transitions is enhanced by neural structure sharing across tasks, saving parameters and training time when added sequentially.
The method's accuracy and parameter efficiency were validated through experiments on complex image datasets compared to state-of-the-art continual learning approaches. A major issue affecting numerous individuals worldwide is intestinal parasitic infections. These infections are primarily transmitted by consuming contaminated food or drinking contaminated water, and can also be spread through intimate contact or bodily fluids. The parasites thrive in the human gastrointestinal tract, causing severe health problems if left untreated. Consequently, a timely diagnosis is critical to prevent the progression of these infections. The standard approach to diagnosing intestinal parasites involves a microscopic examination, but this method has drawbacks, as it requires an expert operator and can be time-consuming, often leading to false negatives. A novel, efficient, and accurate diagnostic method based on Deep Belief Networks has been developed for categorizing intestinal parasites. The proposed system excels in its ability to classify a wide array of parasites as well as eggs and larvae, achieving a high accuracy of 98.1% with a compact feature set, thus making it a feasible solution for clinical diagnosis. The methodology and examination results are presented in detail. Additionally, this research provides a comprehensive review of intestinal intestinal parasites, highlighting their causes, modes of transmission, symptoms, complications, and commonality in tropical countries. The study also highlights the importance of timely diagnosis and treatment to prevent severe health consequences. The proposed Deep Belief Network approach offers a promising insight into the development of future intestinal parasite diagnosis systems. The dataset also includes predicted classification labels for each specimen and corresponding thumbnail images. The research aims to contribute towards the development of future diagnostic systems. The PALEOCCENE project's primary objective is to develop and utilizing PAI experiments in low-energy contexts, specifically for detecting low-energy direct nuclear recoil measurements.  Based on existing research, a prototype system utilizing a PAI crystal and silicon-based components is proposed for direct detection of nuclear recoil measurements.  This prototype would feature multi-energy channels, along with customized processing techniques, in order to differentiate between nuclear and non-nuclear events.  Furthermore, a corresponding simulation-based analysis is suggested for extracting the recoil rate from such experiments.  This method would involve multiple factors including the time, specific energy, and event type of recoil events.  This approach would also allow for various factors to be taken into account in order to reduce non-relevant event types while increasing the sensitivity of recoil rate measurements.  Finally, the PALEOCCENE team aims to develop and test an actual prototype utilizing a $^{100}$Mo-based target, in order to demonstrate its capabilities for extracting the recoil rate.  This ultimate goal is for the PALEOCENE project to contribute significantly to the development of future large-scale direct detection experiments that rely on PAI technology.  In particular the PALEOCENE team aims to enable these future experiments to achieve the capability to discover both neutrinoless double beta decay and the so-called WIMPs, which is a key scientific goal in the field.  This future capability would result in essentially zero counted rates for recoil and non-recoil types over a 300 day counting period, with the ability to achieve this goal by reducing rates to 1 count per 300 day period.  This extremely low rate of 1 count per 300 day period is essentially a measure of experimental purity, with the ability to achieve this extremely low rate by removing all relevant factors that could contribute to counted rates for the particular experiment in question.  By doing this analysis the PALEOCENE team was able to identify a number of potential technical areas for future improvement in low energy PAI technology, with the ultimate goal of establishing a systematic way that future low energy PAI technology can use the PAI principle to reduce the rates to a very low level by identifying and modeling all relevant factors that could contribute to counted rates for the particular experiment in question. In the initial stages of an epidemic, the disease spreads among a limited number of individuals and can be visualized as emerging clusters on a graph representing the infected population. A significant amount of research has been conducted on the macro-level spreading dynamics, such as how the epidemic grows and at what speed it spreads, through mathematical theories and models. However, there is a significant gap in the understanding of a more micro-level aspect of an epidemic, specifically, how the initial clusters form and how the disease spreads through these early-stage clusters. To fill this knowledge gap, a groundbreaking research proposes an innovative method to study and define these early-stage clusters geometrically on networks, such as street maps, and evaluate the effectiveness of the spread by examining their dimensions. In this study, a clustering geometry is used to identify and define these early-stage clusters geometrically on networks, and a new analysis method and tool are developed to study the growth and development of these clusters geometrically, based on the spread of the disease through these clusters. A assessment test using simulated data reveals that the proposed method offers more precise and accurate predictions of an epidemic by analyzing the geometric properties of these clusters, such as their construction, growth, and development, and their effectiveness in the spread of the disease. This new method further enables the evaluation of the impact of different measures and policies by analyzing their effectiveness in altering these early-stage clusters and the spread of the disease. A real-world case study of the COVID-19 pandemic in Contagem, Brazil during 2020 is conducted to verify the feasibility, utility, and impact of the proposed geometric analysis method, and its practical applications in the predictions and measurements of an epidemic. The research demonstrates that the proposed geometric analysis method offers more detailed and accurate micro-level insights into the formation and spread of these early-stage clusters and the initial stages of an epidemic. A groundbreaking network geometry algorithm is developed to identify and analyze the spread of these early-stage clusters geometrically, and its corresponding tool, called epidemic-forest, is available online for the community to reproduce these findings. The research demonstrates its feasibility, utility, and impact and opens up new avenues for the predictions and measurements of an epidemic during the initial stages. The proposed geometric analysis method further offers more precise and detailed micro-level insights into the early-stage clusters and the initial stages of an epidemic. A groundbreaking research proposal for the predictions and measurements of an epidemic during the initial stages is presented in the thesis, and its main contributions are summarized in the conclusion. The research community is invited to reproduce these findings and further advance this line

Natural language can be employed to specify objectives in reinforcement learning environments, although this is hindered by the lack of a predetermined syntax and the potential for ambiguous interpretation. Current methods that rely on natural language are typically limited to compact, syntactically simple input, while more complex inputs requiring grammatical structure are often beyond their reach. A proposed solution to this problem involves inducing a latent representation of the task by means of a transformer architecture, incorporating a dataset of manually written descriptions, and using teacher-student training to reach a state of optimal performance. As demonstrated, this method enables the successful completion of tasks defined by natural language, even when described in a manner that demands a more sophisticated grammatical understanding, whereas a method relying on natural language without the employment of a latent representation fails to overcome the associated ambiguities. Additionally, experiments have shown this technique to be particularly effective for less familiar tasks, whereas compact inputs pose relatively fewer challenges. Quantum channels represent a fundamental component of quantum information processing, consisting in a sequence of linear transformations on the space of quantum states that preserve the probability norm. Extensive research has been conducted on the topic of state tomography, leading to its complete characterization under certain constraints. This study focuses on the feasibility of tomographing quantum channels through the utilization of quantum state tomography results. Specifically, we establish that for any quantum channel, there exists an extensive set of at most two-state shadow opertors that can accurately reproduce the channel's characteristics. Moreover, we demonstrate that for a specific class of quantum channels, including unital quantum channels, optimal reproduction is guaranteed with exactly two-state shadow operators. This achievement is verified through a detailed analysis of two-state shadow tomography for a unital free unitary channel, a unimodular quantum channel, a semidefinite quantum channel, and a trace-preserving quantum channel. Moreover, we show that the number of two-state shadow operators required for accurate channel reproduction is inversely related to the channel's dimension and we derive exact mathematical expressions for this connection. This work has important implications for the practical implementation of quantum information processing, enabling the use of established and proven methods for quantum state tomography to accurately characterize and diagnose quantum channels. Moreover, our results empower the implementation of automated tools for accurate channel diagnosis and applications in quantum debugging and testing. The growing reliance on Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) as mobile platforms for visual sensing is necessitating the development of more efficient automation techniques. Our paper focuses on UAV path optimization for time-sensitive visual sensing applications, where the UAV is equipped with a camera capturing images sequenced by a controller. Unlike conventional UAV models relying on the positional relationship between the camera and features, our approach treats the images as a time-ordered sequence, independent of spatial 3D features. This allows us to apply techniques from online planning theory, leveraging the simplicity of the exposure-burst action that significantly reduces the computational complexity. Our approach is implemented on a UAV with the deep learning-based, sequential image exposure policy called Exposure-Maximizing Action Policy, as described in the paper. Our experimental results demonstrate the computational efficiency and effectiveness of our approach under diverse, practical scenarios. For instance, on a desktop with a GPU processing power of 3.7 GHz, our Exposure-Maximizing Action Policy allows the UAV to plan and expose 100 image exposures in approximately 0.5 seconds. Moreover, our Exposure-Maximizing Action Policy, when autonomously flying while exposing image bursts, achieves a 5-fold reduction in the overall energy consumption compared to the standard approach. Our Exposure-Maximizing Action Policy has also been successfully tested on a 12 minute, 350 image exposure sequence, while flying and exposing image bursts continuously, as shown in the accompanying video at https://youtu.be/UyGQsOJ0wMM. This achievement marks a new milestone in the autonomous, prolonged-lasting, aerodynamic, and sensing beam-powered UAV development, as reported in a recent journal paper. In general, our Exposure-Maximizing Action Policy provides a versatile, efficient, and effective strategy to tackle a wide array of time-constrained, mobile computer vision applications, as highlighted in the related work section, as the fastest and most straightforward exposure planning approach among the top-ranked candidates, as per the tableau-based exposure planning methods summary. In the future, our Exposure-Maximizing Action Policy is designed to integrate the exposure sequence with the positional, spatial, temporal, and social dynamics of the sensing beam to expand the scope of the exposure planning category, as proposed in the related work section. In addition, our approach is also considered a pioneering work to integrate the autonomous sensing beam and the exposure sequence, as highlighted in the related work section. Network centrality metrics quantify node importance using various geometric and diffusive characteristics, focusing on distinct spatial and temporal scales.  From a geometric perspective, the centrality of a node gauges its proximity to other nodes within its surrounding area, whereas from a diffusive perspective, it reflects the efficiency of information dissemination.  The node-centric and graph-centric views of centrality are characterized by different scales - the former is microscopically localized to individual nodes or their immediate neighborhoods, whereas the latter is macrosocial in scope, covering the entire network.  However, the chartable centrality landscape remains uncharted for the macroscopic network view.  To bridge this gap, the authors introduce a new centrality metric called Gromov centrality, measuring the deviation of shortest path distances from triangle inequality inequalities. A new technique based on the variational free energy provides an accurate representation of complex datasets in a low-dimensional space. It does so by employing a generative model, which is composed of multiple layers of mean and variance estimators, necessary for computing the variational free energy. We refer to this generative model as the deep generative encoder, as it is utilized in an encoder-decoder system. In this study, we examine the behavior of the DGME during optimal adaptation to a dataset generated by a mixed distribution, consisting of two distinct components with varying densities. Specifically, we analyze a situation in which a dataset contains a large, sparsely populated region surrounded by two densely populated areas. We observe how the DGME develops structures that comprise compactly supported layers in the representation and generative streams, with corresponding increases in the log-likelihood at these representations and generative parameters. We show that the density of these regions can be estimated directly from the optimal DGME parameters through a new variational free energy. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of our findings from both theoretical and practical perspectives and examine the challenges of implementing the DGME framework. We also explore the limitations of the new estimator, comparing its performance to existing approaches on synthetic and real-world datasets in hand-written digit recognition and unsupervised image generation tasks. The results demonstrate that the new estimator achieves state-of-the-art performance with improved generalization and image generation capabilities. One of the key advantages of the DGME framework is its ability to reverse the normal workflow of standard autoencoders, allowing us to design new classes of autoencoders that require optimal adaptation of the DGME model. We examine the behavior of these encoders, starting with a simplified version of the standard denoising encoder and gradually increasing the complexity by introducing generative capabilities to the stream. We also discuss how the DGME framework can be used to estimate and manipulate the structure of the representation and generative streams through various perturbation techniques. Specifically, we examine three perturbation techniques: predictive perturbations, to improve hand-written digit classification; generative perturbations, to introduce noise into the latent space of an autoencoder trained on the MNIST dataset; and perturbative variational free energy perturbations, to estimate and directly read out the density of the mixed distribution in a dataset generated by a mixed distribution with two distinct components. Overall, we believe that the new DGME framework has the potential to significantly contribute to the development of new image and representation learning techniques. Recently, the focus of unsupervised speech synthesis has been on fast and efficient approaches, leading to research based on autoencoders. However, the existing autoencoder models are often modified from supervised speech synthesis frameworks, which includes a significant frame-level cost function, the loss of important speech attributes, and the inability to replicate human-like sequence-level errors. In response to these issues, a new autoencoder framework has been developed that can be used for unsupervised speech synthesis, which is inspired by the sequence-to-sequence approach. The framework consists of two main components, one responsible for generating speech waveforms from text, and another for creating a voice-specific representation of acoustics from speech, both connected through a voice-specific representation encoder. In contrast to existing autoencoder models, this new framework allows for the inclusion of speech attributes, as well as errors at the sequence level, which enables more accurate speech synthesis. In addition, this new framework has been enhanced with a modification to its speech synthesis algorithm to produce higher quality outcomes, which involves the use of a dynamic window for reducing repeated speech inputs, as well as the inclusion of a sequence-level loss function to mimic the natural errors in speech, which leads to significant performance improvements. The results of our study demonstrate that this new framework can effectively produce speech from text in an unsupervised setting, which outperforms the existing speech synthesis models both qualitatively and quantitatively, by producing more natural speech with improved audibility and coherence. Aspect-based sentiment analysis focuses on determining the sentiment of a specific aspect within product reviews. Previous studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of representation-based methods in this field, where the representation of an aspect or review closely relates to the sentiment target. This paper proposes that the sentiment target also embodies implicit emotion, which is explored through supervised contrastive pre-training. By combining reviews and sentiment targets in a sentence embedding space, contrastive learning captures the correlation between them, subsequently retuning the sentence representation to better capture implicit emotion. Recent studies have examined the capacity of language models to process visual information and how this affects their performance in visual-centric tasks such as image description. However, there is a gap in understanding how language models utilize visual inputs when engaged in open-domain writing tasks like generating short stories or novels. We propose an approach where a language model is supplemented with a vision module that provides explicit visual cues in the form of control tokens. The model is then trained to represent these visual inputs within its parameter space, mirroring the technique used in diffusion models. The experimental results demonstrate that incorporating visual cues into language generation leads to more coherent and naturally flowing text outputs, as evidenced by improvements in both the coherence and continuity metrics. Notably, human evaluators also consider the generated outputs produced by this method as more natural and enjoyable to read. This paper presents a novel optimization technique called AskewSGD to efficiently train deep neural networks with quantized weights. Initially, we transform the quantized neural network into an integer-based model, which we then tackle as a combinatorial optimization problem. Our AskewSGD algorithm develops a continuous, differentiable variant of this optimization challenge and provides a dual iteration approach - first, inner iterations progress through the quantized distribution, accompanied by a regular SGD update for outer iterations. Our tests on various networks, including MobileNetV2 and ResNet51, demonstrate that AskewSGD surpasses existing methods like LDI and SLIM by a significant margin, even when allowing them additional computational resources to sample distributions. Our AskewSGD implementation is now freely accessible on the GitHub platform.

Contrastive learning loss optimizes image classification by learning informative, discriminative features through negative example manipulation. We find that the specific structure of the loss function influences the quality and diversity of the features generated. Our analysis reveals that supervised contrastive learning loss extracts distinct features from each class example, causing classification to rely heavily on semantic features and minimizing reliance on random signals. This design, however, hinders the model's ability to distinguish between hard pairs, resulting in inferior performance when encountered. We establish a theoretical model to predict performance based on the proportion of semantic features, and propose multiple methods for balancing feature extraction, including adjusting input mixtures and model training configurations, to improve performance and foster multitask compatibility when applying contrastive learning loss in collaboration with traditional cross-entropy loss. Our findings are validated across multiple datasets and various head architectures. The accompanying code can be accessed at https://github.com/songkong/contrastive_clf. In this work, we explore certain properties of hyper-invariant MERA, a specific type of quantum circuit, and its potential applications within adiabatic quantum computing. By utilizing four distinct parameters - alpha, beta, gamma, and delta - we can fully characterize the Mermin map, Mermin density operator, and their characteristics, as well as establish parametric definitions for the majority of a hyper-invariant MERA's pyramidal substructure. Our findings also outline specific protocols for obtaining essential circuit elements, such as gamma- and delta-identity gates. We further establish that hyper-invariant MERMs can't be expressed using Kitaev's ZZZ-gates, and instead, we determine the necessary and sufficient conditions for realizing hyper-invariant MERMAs using a single parameter, which in turn facilitates the derivation of universal computing principles. Our research focuses on the cost of achieving this universality and demonstrates that certain dependencies with parameters alpha and beta will lead to achievable goals, which is consistent with the universal principles we've established. We have also examined the speed of the adiabatic evolution within hyper-invariant MERMAs based on parameter gamma. Our results indicate that hyper-invariant MERMAs provide an effective framework for achieving fast and efficient evolution through the adiabatic principle. We intend for our work on hyper-invariant MERMAs to lay the groundwork for novel quantum computing architectures, which we have explored and discussed. These future architectures will allow for compact, adaptable, and efficient implementation of quantum information systems. They are based on our understanding that quantum systems can be viewed as complex adaptations of lower-level quantum interactions, which is an idea we have explored at length. Additionally, we have established connections between hyper-invariant MERMAs and certain holographic error correction systems that possess unique power-law dependencies, which is an area of study and investigation for future work. Developing text generation models for dialogue systems poses unique challenges, given that human communication involves not only conveying information but also establishing relationships and maintaining social bonds. Prior work on dialogue generation focuses primarily on language generation, whereas, according to Halliday, this type of generation corresponds to only one aspect of communication. In contrast, a more comprehensive model is proposed - the LEATHER model - which incorporates systemic functional principles from systemic functional linguistics. According to these principles, dialogue is characterized by three dimensions, including relationships, information, and social dimensions. A multi-task approach is proposed to capture relationships through an embedded generative grammar model, while the information and social dimensions are addressed through information ranking and coherence tasks. Additionally, a dataset is being developed for evaluation purposes. In experiments with a limited dataset, the proposed model exhibits improved performance in terms of its ability to establish relationships with others, and further analysis is provided to illustrate its capabilities and potential avenues for future research. Evaluation results demonstrate that the proposed model performs better at natural language generation. Following Quantum Chromodynamics' 1972 formulation, a breakthrough in its regularization came when Kenneth Wilson applied it to Euclidean lattices. This opened doors for in-depth calculations of QCD's properties, especially its phase diagram. Over two decades, these studies, primarily based on plain lattices, revealed that QCD has a critical point and explores the phase with deconfining properties. Introducing dynamical fermions slowed this process, but even with them, QCD's thermal phase is similar to that of lattice gauge theory without quarks. In complex scenarios like heavy ion collisions, however, QCD is not in its thermal state; it's in a state of quark-gluon plasma along with a complex vacuum of quarks and gluons. To understand this vacuum and the plasma, we need precise corrections, especially close to the critical point. This contribution is a comprehensive review on using lattices to study QCD, focusing on temperature and density variations. It will cover key findings on QCD's critical point, the hadron-to-plasma transition, quark-gluon plasma,, and the complex vacuum of quarks and gluons. It will also outline the theoretical methods to study these issues and recent progress. Moreover, we'll discuss how these studies, primarily based on plain lattices, can be applied to understand heavy ion collisions within the framework of QCD. This review will also cover the impact of the U(1) phase transformation on lattice studies of QCD and novel lattice structures to explore this issue. Finally, we'll discuss whether these lattice studies can be generalized to other four-fermion models. Although this contribution is primarily on QCD, we hope that the methods and achievements might also contribute to other gauge-theories with fermions. It is also possible to extend these studies to other areas of quantum field theories. Please note that we'll mainly use plain lattice models in this contribution, but some more advanced lattice structures are discussed at the end. Moreover, we'll mainly concentrate on four-fermion models, but we'll also briefly discuss other potential generalizations. Further studies are needed to understand these extensions. Predicting the long-term lifespan of offshore wind turbines requires precise analysis of the harsh marine environment's impact on the turbines. Accurate predictions are hindered by the limitations of computational simulations and the scarcity of extensive real-world data, creating a significant engineering hurdle. To bridge this gap, we focus on modeling the probabilistic deterioration of specific wind turbine components due to predicted stresses, which are in turn influenced by the uncertainties of measured wind and sea states. To address this issue, we employ Gaussian Process regression for two tasks: first, matching the statistics of downstream modeling tasks, and second, simulating the variability of sequential observations. Our methodology, which leverages previously identified regression techniques, demonstrates an average percentage error of about 10 compared to computational simulations for the deterioration of lubricant in gearbox bearings. Furthermore, we note that our methodology assumes that the temporal effects of stress variations on a wind turbine are significant, an assumption that has been empirically verified through analysis of measured data. Our methodology's main advantage is that it generates probabilistic forecasts of a wind turbine's lifespan, thereby providing a comprehensive framework for offshore wind-farms with the inclusion of spatial variability and sequential temporal effects. For instance, our analysis shows that the probabilistic deterioration of lubricant in a gearbox increases by about 30% when the frequency of stress variations in the y-direction is doubled. Moreover, our results demonstrate that the probabilistic lifespan of a bearing is extended by about 10-20 years when the frequency of stress variations in the y-direction is doubled or the amplitude of stress variations in the x-direction is increased by a factor of 2 and 3, respectively. Our work has significant implications for the analysis of sequential data with the application of Gaussian Process regression, an area that requires further research.
