The global spread of the 2019 COVID-19 pandemic caused by SARS-CoV-2 has resulted in widespread losses and societal disruption, with the aim of mitigating its impact many countries have implemented measures such as isolation, as well as tracing contacts of infected individuals. To facilitate this process, governments have developed mobile apps that help identify people who may have come into close proximity with those who have tested positive for the virus, enhancing public safety by reducing the disease's spread and saving lives.

These contact tracing mobile apps have gained significant traction across the globe, exemplified by countries like the UK, Singapore, and China successfully utilizing them to contain outbreaks. However, concerns have been raised regarding users' personal data, as numerous apps have been labeled as non-compliant with the European Union's (EU) General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) due to failing to honor anonymity, as well as comply with the GDPR's consent requirements. Moreover, users have been coerced into downloading and using these contact tracing apps by being threatened with disciplinary action, police scrutiny, or even detention, as reported in countries such as China.

To illustrate the issue of balancing public safety with personal data protection, a novel instance of the well-known conceptual model, Coronavirus-SUS, has been introduced, based on the understanding that Coronavirus-SUS is a composite of five distinct components, specifically User, Sensor, User's Environment, Risk Management, and Administrator. This conceptual model serves as a reliable tool for examining the inherent properties of contact tracing systems, ultimately enabling designers and developers to design contact tracing systems that are compliant with data protection regulations, while safeguarding users' anonymity, as echoed by the recent EU Court of Justice ruling regarding the Irish Data Protection Commissioner's case against Facebook. Notwithstanding the above-mentioned design principles, a secure contact tracing mobile app implementation that provides sufficient anonymity and compliance composites is also proposed. This implementation, based on the Coronavirus-SUS instance, incorporates a novel composite called Anonymous-SUS, specifically designed to ensure privacy preservation, while providing the necessary safety guarantees, as exemplified by the European Commission's recent request to the NetEnabling Technologies Scientific and Technical Advisory Group to develop a contact tracing technology that is compliant with the GDPR.

Ramanujan formulated a complex equation involving odd zeta values and hypergeometric expressions, which was later generalized into a form involving the Hurwitz zeta function. Our work connects the generalized form to the Weierstrass sigma and zeta functions of specific half-plane arguments. We also introduce a specific identity derived from the product of two Hurwitz zeta functions, focused on odd zeta values. Furthermore, we introduce a family of equations similar to Ramanujan's, applicable to broader families of hypergeometric expressions. Several examples are provided to illustrate the equations for specific cases. Building upon Ramanujan's work, we have expanded it to cover all odd zeta values, a significant advancement in this area. As an additional benefit, we have obtained new identities for the Weierstrass sigma and zeta functions corresponding to arguments of the form $2\pi e^{i\theta}$. We examine the phenomenon of analytic continuation in the context of complex statistical mechanics. To extend analytical results from one manifold to another, we investigate the conditions under which this extension is possible. Our study, centered on a specific landscape known as the deformed skew plane, yields insights into extending analytical findings. We then apply these conditions to systems of bosons and fermions, revealing a broader principle: the principle of electric neutrality. Our work also reveals that many well-known solutions in real statistical mechanics have hidden underlying structures that can be uncovered through the lens of analytic continuation. We demonstrate that these solutions can be unified into a single, consistent framework by employing an adjusted version of the modified Bessel function, appropriately modified for fermionic systems. Our findings provide a theoretical basis for extending analytical results, complemented by empirical examples illustrating the concept of electric neutrality. Specifically, we show that electric neutrality conditions can expose latent structures in both Gaussian and Polya distributions. Moreover, our study reveals that these distributions are interconnected and can be unified into a single, consistent framework characterized by the modified Bessel function, applicable to both bosonic and fermionic systems. The complementarity between analytical continuation and the principles governing its conditions offers a fresh perspective on statistical mechanics and the principles underlying the method of analytic continuation. Our work may inspire the development of new techniques for uncovering latent structures in a wide range of fields, including physics, mathematics, and computational systems. To facilitate the translation of our findings to these fields, we provide a collection of intuitive examples that illustrate the concept of electric neutrality and its potential applications. Moreover, our study suggests that the principle of electric neutrality may serve as a bridge linking information theory and the emergence of latent structures, an area of research that may yield significant breakthroughs in the near future. Light field technology is currently an active area of research with numerous applications across optics and computer vision, including free-view-point video and view switching applications. However, the high dimensionality of light field data and its resulting redundancy, particularly in lateral directions, necessitates data reduction through compression. This paper focuses on developing a compression framework that is feasible in practice and considers the inherent characteristics of light field patterns. This approach differs from existing methods, such as those based on deep learning, by proposing a novel theoretical foundation. This foundation highlights the significance of two factors during light field compression: the disparity between adjacent views and the lateral coherence within a slice. These factors are then utilized to develop a compression framework consisting of two stages. First, a parity check matrix-based algorithm compresses and eliminates redundant data. This is followed by a convolutional neural network-based decoder, powered by an angular image regression network, to reconstruct the compressed data. This decoder uses the theoretical framework's proposed check patterns and hierarchical encoding to pinpoint defective data blocks. This paper showcases the efficacy of this method by applying it to 4K, 8K, and 8K x3 light field videos. Furthermore, the results of the experiments demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses the performance of the state-of-the-art approaches while achieving comparable outcomes for the baseline approaches with reduced complexity. Various atmospheric models employed in atmospheric dispersion compensation have distinct features that need to be taken into consideration. These models fall into two categories: those based on empirical formulas or those driven by numerical calculations of atmospheric conditions. Empirical models rely on established relationships between the effects of a reference atmospheric layer on light passing through it, as observed at a specific site. On the other hand, numerical models simulate the atmospheric conditions for a designated latitude and can account for dynamic changes in atmospheric dispersion over a wider range of zenith angles. When precise values of atmospheric dispersion are essential, as they are in adaptive systems, the accuracy of the atmospheric model used becomes particularly significant. In this paper, a detailed analysis of the atmospheric models' characteristics will be presented, along with the discussion of the implications of utilizing these models to calculate atmospheric dispersion for a fixed altitude. Ultimately, we hope that this work inspires the development of more powerful AI-based solutions that can effectively mitigate the impact of external interference in IRS-assisted wireless-powered networks, thereby seamlessly integrating these technologies into existing wireless-powered networks, ultimately leading to substantial performance enhancements with low computational complexity. Advanced economies have experienced rising life spans over the past century. A significant factor behind increased lifespan has been the reduced mortality rate among seniors. However, in the past two decades, improvements in lifespan have started to waver. Research on forecasted age-specific mortality rates suggests that this slowing trend is likely to continue. A recent theory proposes that reductions in mortality rates are influenced by long-term variations in factors such as income, education, and medical advancement. These factors can create fluctuations in age-specific risk profiles - particularly the disparity between infant and elderly mortality - without necessarily affecting individual lifetime risk. Considering that advancements in medical technology and changes in elderly-specific lifestyle factors can contribute to increased lifespan, it is likely that the distance between infant and elderly mortality rates serves as a key indicator of a country's economic development. With this in mind, we have developed a two-component mortality model based on multiple-factor influences, which suggests that countries with higher infant mortality rates will ultimately experience increased elderly mortality rates. Our model has demonstrated capacity for long-term predictions of mortality rates, yielding relatively low RE-levels metro area variations. However, the model's performance in precise predictions of mortality fluctuations during times of rapid change is still somewhat limited. A simulation revealed that, when accounting for temporal variations in factor loadings, predicted variance of RE-life expectancy at birth was roughly double that of a model with static factor loadings. Furthermore, a multi-model analysis revealed that, when accounting for temporal variations in factor loadings, simulated mean life expectancy increased by approximately 0.5 years each decade. However, the model's effectiveness in precisely forecasting life expectancy fluctuations during times of significant change - such as the 1970s and 2008 financial crises - still needs to be improved. We plan to integrate machine learning techniques into our model to enhance its capacity for accurately forecasting short-term fluctuations in mortality rates. A deeper understanding of factors contributing to increased lifespan and their interplay with remaining disparities in age-specific risk profiles will be essential in developing a revised model that can effectively predict both long-term and short-term trends in mortality rates. Our findings highlight the need for increased focus on reducing disparities in risk profiles, particularly those affecting seniors and young children. Reducing these disparities could be an important step in mitigating the impact of demographic change on future mortality rates. Our investigation reveals that the prediction errors in NAS are significant, with the prediction deviation ranging from 10% to 200% for popular NAS benchmarks. Such inaccuracies are the primary cause of high costs in NAS. To mitigate this issue, we propose a simple approach called prediction error-guided sampling (PGES), where models are prioritized for evaluation based on their predicted performance. Our experiments demonstrate that PGES reduces the average training cost of NAS by 52%-65% while maintaining or even improving the performance of state-of-the-art NAS methods on various benchmarks. Machine translation's reliability assessment of translators is usually based on evaluating the consistency of their work through a measure of translation accuracy, typically calculated as the precise ratio of translation. While this approach may seem effective for identifying unreliable translators, it has a significant drawback: it only accounts for accurate translations and disregards the relevance of incorrect translations in assessing reliability. Furthermore, this straightforward method relies on previous knowledge of a translator's past work, which is often not available in many situations. To overcome these limitations, a Bayesian technique is proposed to classify translators based on translation accuracy in a specific domain, by evaluating both the frequencies of accurate and inaccurate translations. To this end, a translator's reliability score is calculated as the ratio of accurate translations to the total number of translations in a given text, by sampling from two probability distributions, one containing accurate translations and the other containing inaccurate translations. Unlike traditional methods, this approach considers the roles of incorrect translations in assessing reliability. Moreover, reliability can be assessed even without prior knowledge of a translator's past work by using statistical information about the given text. To demonstrate the efficacy of this method, two experiments were conducted. First, a simulation study was carried out to verify the proposed method's robustness to varying levels of reliability, and to compare its performance with the traditional method. A second experiment classified the translators in the JRC-Aquarius dataset using the proposed method. Results showed that the proposed method outperformed the traditional method by ensuring higher reliability scores for accurate translators and lower reliability scores for inaccurate translators. In addition, the proposed method was more robust to diverse reliability levels. In summary, a new Bayesian technique is introduced for the assessment of machine translators' reliability, by considering both accurate and inaccurate translations in a translator's work. Furthermore, this method is shown to be more robust and reliable than traditional approaches. Lastly, a demonstration of the proposed method's performance was achieved by classifying translators in the JRC-Aquarius dataset. We hope the proposed method can be applied in various contexts such as finding the most reliable translators or assessing the reliability of machine translation tools. We intend to extend this method to other translation-related tasks. In the context of buying tickets, a safe investment strategy involves maximizing the expected value of gains without exceeding a set risk threshold. Conversely, the optimal selling strategy involves pricing tickets to maximize revenue while considering the impact of losses. We've discovered that novel processes such as polynomial and umklapp electron-phonon couplings make a significant contribution to valley mixing in 2D materials, a phenomenon that has been overlooked in existing research. This new model reveals that the energy splitting between valley states decreases as the size of the 2D material lattice increases, predicting that a certain type of moire lattice material, specifically TBG graphite, would exhibit valley splitting on a much longer scale than previously suggested by theoretical models, with a potential energy splitting ranging from few MeV to a few hundred MeV. We've also explored how these novel electron-phonon coupling mechanisms influence the selection rule in 2D moire superlattices, showing that umklapp processes can lead to the cancellation of valley mixing in moire superlattices, a result that has experimental and theoretical implications. The VISDA-C dataset, utilized for the NeurIPS 2022 Visual Domain Adaptation challenge, requires adapting a network to a target domain, either CVPR 2022 dataset 'Dogs' or VISDA-C dataset, despite lacking paired source and target images. Two solutions have garnered top accolades for the challenge: 'Late FauxPass' ranking first and 'Early FauxPass' ranking second, both employing GAN-based pseudo-label approaches. Late FauxPass in particular utilized the 'Dogs' dataset to train an unsupervised classifier, then leveraged this classifier in a self-supervised manner for VISDA-C domain adaptation with the 'Dogs' dataset. Next, it generated pseudo-images for VISDA-C using an pre-trained discriminator from the 'Dogs' dataset, ultimately achieving a test accuracy of 69.18% on VISDA-C after a two-step training process. Building upon this framework, the solution further refined its model in a semi-supervised manner with the VISDA-C dataset, ultimately achieving a test accuracy of 72.25%. It's noteworthy that the solution does not employ image cropping, the use of which can yield a test accuracy of 74.84%. Therefore, the solution does not violate the competition's data augmentation constraint. Specifying a point set on the surface of a unit sphere exactly represents the distribution of directions of reflected light coming from a luminous point source located an infinite distance away. To generate an image of the light distribution, we need to accurately represent each point on the sphere with corresponding colors. Building upon earlier work involving colored collections of points, we propose creating colored maps consisting of disjoint surface regions, called polyhedra, which are painted with consistent directional lighting. However, since collecting all necessary information about these directions is impossible and impractical, we develop an algorithm that approximates this light distribution using colored, stitched spherical panels. A panel consists of a polygon with a unique normal vector representing a specific light direction and a unique color, representing the consistent lighting direction in that area. While maintaining consistency in colors, we improve the accuracy of the light distribution map. A fast and approximate algorithm called COOP quickly determines the optimal collection of panel normal vectors, achieving high efficiency by first concentrating on approximating global patterns and then refining local details. Additionally, we develop an algorithm called LOOCO that optimizes each panel's color in coordination with its neighboring panels, resulting in a significant improvement in color accuracy. Our method contributes to a range of applications including spherical image rendering and 3D vector representation. A demonstration of our method's capabilities can be seen in a accompanying video. The updated rev9 mesh router, now employed by hundreds of thousands of users, boasts improved performance and streamlined update process, facilitated by its compact size and quad-core processor. Although the 5 GHz mesh protocol has undergone optimization, we still observe a notable decrease in transfer speeds within our network. A thorough examination revealed that this loss is primarily attributed to the following factors. Firstly, the mesh network uses the DSA algorithm, which sometimes results in inefficient network configuration, reducing transfer efficiency by up to 85%. Secondly, the router's operating system employs the CoAP protocol in the update process, incurring an additional delay of around 4 milliseconds per packet, largely due to its lightweight design. A simulation revealed that using the HTTP protocol instead would increase this delay to approximately 45 milliseconds. Thirdly, the update process involves an intermediate node, causing a further delay of up to 8 milliseconds in each direction. We recommend the adoption of the following measures to enhance the transfer process. To improve efficiency, mesh networks should prioritize keeping the client, server, and intermediate node in the same subnetwork. To minimize latency, the update process could make greater use of packet bundling and caching techniques. To increase throughput, the update sequence could be optimized using the TCP Fast Open and Transmission Credit mechanisms. The German Energy Transition models have been widely utilized to determine the most suitable scenarios for meeting energy needs while minimizing environmental impact. However, the models have been found to produce vastly different results despite being based on similar assumptions, indicating a pressing need to clarify how the models' outputs vary in response to changes in underlying assumptions. This research examines the methodological foundations of ten comprehensive power system expansion models to understand how their key assumptions work and how their output is affected. The models' structures show that most models respond to changes in energy demand, technology costs, and social policy by adjusting variable and fixed investments, with variable investments typically consisting of flexible generation and energy storage. Notably, the models disagree on the role of nuclear power, with some assuming replacement and others assuming coexistence with existing nuclear power plants. This discrepancy has significant implications, with model outputs diverging dramatically under even minor changes in assumptions, particularly in investment scenarios and electricity generation mixes. Consequently, the models' variability in energy storage and nuclear power assumptions leads to considerable differences in energy prices and system efficiency. This analysis highlights the necessity for standardized assumptions and additional output across models to facilitate comparative evaluation, alongside further research to explore the specific scenarios and output outcomes. The variability in model results suggests that models should be evaluated not only based on technical feasibility but also on their ability to produce robust and transferable outcomes that can be applied to a broader range of assumptions and energy scenarios. Furthermore, the models' output could identify and analyze critical points where changes in specific variables have considerable effects on the results, helping to prioritize and implement policies that benefit energy system resilience and variability. The discussion also touches on the potential limitations and biases of the models. For instance, the models' outcomes are often based on technological characteristics rather than the actual performance of specific technologies, with variations in technology characteristics leading to considerable variations in model results. Moreover, the models predominantly focus on system-level rather than device-level variables. This lack of detail leads to considerable uncertainties regarding the spatial distribution of costs and benefits, particularly with regard to the distribution of costs among end-consumers and the spatial feasibility of renewable energy integration. Investigating these issues could significantly advance our understanding of the models' outcomes and help identify and analyze the biasses of specific technologies. Finally, the discussion also highlights the need for more detailed and transparent model input and output files to facilitate communication and collaboration among the various stakeholders involved in energy system modeling and policy-making. In an attempt to better understand this interaction, we propose a new method for extracting design discussions from freely written descriptions of artifacts, and subsequent analysis to determine if conclusion stability correlates with specific emotional and personal traits expressed in these discussions. A significant gap remains in identifying how light Higgs boson components originate from more substantial, heavy partners, specifically within extended new physics models. One such model involves the realization of a new set of elementary fields that combine with the Higgs field to form a triplet of scalar components. These components are not only influenced by the light Higgs boson's resonance, but also by other non-resonant production methods. We examine one such non-resonant manufacturing method in depth, but then shift our focus to a more realistic case where the primary production method is not clearly identifiable. We provide comprehensive production equations for the triplet scalar components and analyze their potential within both effective field theory and in dynamical triplet scalar models. Our analysis concludes that, despite the complexity when trying to identify the primary production method in the later case, the triplet scalar's properties are still are constrained rather tightly. These constraints can be found at values of $\mathcal{O}(2\text{ TeV})$ for the lightest triplet scalar's mass and $\mathcal{O}(10)$ for its coupling strength at their respective limits. The growth of the web has led to an increase in data storage, with vast amounts of data becoming machine-readable through standardized formats like RDF and ontologies, creating a challenge for language understanding and generation as machines struggle to process knowledge independently. Previous studies have relied on external knowledge retrieval, SPARQL queries, or integrated global memory, but these approaches pose issues like dependent libraries, query results available only online, or memory overload. To address this, a novel architecture is proposed for SPARQL neural machine translation by introducing a centralized knowledge management system that stores knowledge base data as graph structures, allowing for efficient query copying and access. This paper demonstrates the efficacy of this architecture in enhancing translation performance, particularly when dealing with large knowledge graphs, and discusses the benefits and limitations of this approach. Furthermore, it highlights potential applications in improving translation quality, such as leveraging the system as a state-of-the-art knowledge base to improve language generation. Experimental results are provided to support the proposed architecture. This study is a significant contribution to the field of SPARQL neural machine translation as it addresses a major drawback by offering an all-in-one solution for translating SPARQL queries while improving translation performance and efficiency. Moreover, it expands knowledge relevant to SPARQL neural machine translation, focusing on the resource and algorithm levels, to enable the use of large knowledge graphs, thereby advancing the quality of this study and its potential real-world applications. Finally, this study's findings have implications for future research, shedding light on the potential advantages and limitations of this architecture, and encouraging the development of more efficient and machine-learning-based solutions for translating SPARQL queries in the future. Research venues are instrumental in communicating research impacts, yet little attention has been focused on their measurement methods. For decades, citation-based metrics have been used to assess research quality, but they are subject to significant flaws. In contrast, we explore using venue influence measures, which have previously been underrepresented in research on scientific metrics. We develop a simple yet effective method for calculating the influence of conference venues, demonstrating its effectiveness with a case study of three major computer science events. Our findings reveal substantial variations in the influence of these events and highlight their distinct characteristics. These results suggest that venue influence measures could serve as a reliable alternative to citation-based metrics, particularly when accompanied by a multi-dimensional approach to evaluating research quality and impact. The resulting framework enables researchers and readers to make more informed decisions and strategic plans, while also enabling evaluations based on the broader goals of sustainable scientific publishing, such as the environmental impact of the GTC. Our methodology is available for further development and refinement at https://github.com/thesmet/jcsm. The associated code for the case study is also provided at https://github.com/thesmet/venue-influence. The study was conducted with limited financial support, underscoring the need for future research to fund more comprehensive analyses. In the interest of accelerating scientific innovation, we encourage further development of our proposed venue influence measures and related research. Deep learning methods have achieved significant success in numerous applications within the past two decades. Recently, these methods have been applied in control engineering to overcome traditional issues, yet the lack of approaches to quantify their reliability creates obstacles in integrating them into large-scale industrial systems, which heavily rely on validation. It is evident that the conventional validation methods for control systems cannot be directly used for deep learning methods. This paper argues that to effectively utilize deep learning methods in control engineering, a new validation framework specifically designed for deep learning is required. This framework should address two primary goals: the validation of point estimates and the validation of confidence intervals. The main contribution of this study is a novel validation framework for neural networks in the control domain, which uses bootstrapping to achieve this purpose. We demonstrate the practical application of this framework through the evaluation of three examples. The first example is a straightforward one to demonstrate the fundamental concepts of the proposed framework, the second is a scenario-based approach, and the third is a more realistic scenario without prior knowledge of the truth for validation purposes. The results of the study indicate that the proposed framework can successfully validate point estimates and confidence intervals for neural networks in control engineering. This represents a significant step towards the widespread adoption of deep learning techniques in industrial control systems. The proposed framework provides quantitative insights into the reliability of neural networks in control engineering, which enables the selection of neural networks with satisfactory performance and suitable levels of risk in industrial applications. This study sheds light on the importance of the role of validation in control engineering. The scope of this study is limited to neural networks in control engineering and can be extended to other domains where validation is crucial. The framework and methods employed in this study do not rely on specific assumptions regarding the distribution of data, which makes this study applicable to a wide range of problems. Clustering is a crucial technique used for data analysis in numerous fields. For the sake of interpretation, it is often desired that resulting clusters have meaningfully connected boundaries, accounted for overlap regions, and form a logical hierarchy. Unfortunately, common clustering methods do not naturally convey such relationships between adjacent clusters or thoroughly consider the influence of nearby areas. Building on top of the existing fuzzy-$k$-means algorithm, we developed a method that produces a logical hierarchy with overlapping, structured clusters. By utilizing fuzzy clustering, we initially define a concept of nearness to multiple clusters, and then iteratively refine this association in a way that generates a logical cluster structure. We represent this process as a functor representing the relationship between groups in different layers of the hierarchy. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through numerical experiments on dataset samples. Our implementation is available on GitHub under https://github.com/demircioglu/functorial_clustering. The resulting logical clusters can be visually represented using LogGraph, a visualizations tool available at https://github.com/demircioglu/log_graph. The presented approach has potential applications in modeling real-world groupings, such as the formation of flocks of birds or ranks in the military. Given that the method focuses on the structure of the clusters, it may also be used to create artificial, simulated groupings for the purposes of testing. To achieve an efficient and high-quality reconstruction process that operates in real-time, we have developed a pioneering technique called Patch Tracking-based Streaming Tensor Loop Completion (PT-STLC). This approach employs a patch-tracking mechanism to enhance learning resilience and ensure accurate and streamlined learning. Furthermore, PT-STLC leverages the shared knowledge of multiple patches to optimize data recovery from random missing values, while maintaining real-time functionality. Experimental evaluations using diverse video datasets demonstrate the superior performance of PT-STLC in terms of its ability to handle streaming inputs and achieve better results compared to existing methods. Additionally, the simplicity and efficiency of PT-STLC allow it to operate in real-time, making it well-suited for various vision data recovery applications. This study provides the first numerical evidence for the Zakharov-Kolmogorov range in wave turbulence, a theory which predicts a specific frequency spectrum in a particular range of scales. Using the Balitsky equation, we simulated homogeneous, isotropic two-dimensional wave turbulence in a square domain with free-slip boundaries, allowing for the examination of scales up to the Nyquist frequency. We plotted the dimensionless spectral density against the dimensionless wavenumber and observed the Balitsky spectrum's validity at high wavenumbers, as well as an energy transfer instability below a critical wavenumber. Within this critical scale and the Zakharov-Kolmogorov range, our simulations showed consistent spectral densities at varying initial condition configurations. An energy preservation law was also verified in our simulations, confirming that the dimensionless spectral density at high wavenumbers is independent of initial conditions and scale-invariant. Furthermore, our simulations revealed the emergence of the Balitsky spectrum and instability at decreasing wavenumbers with increasing frequencies and increasing numbers of spatial grid points, enabling the verification of the Zakharov-Kolmogorov frequency-scaled spectral formula. This formula was found to be valid in three-dimensional simulations as well. In general, our simulations showed excellent energy preservation in both two-dimensional and three-dimensional wave turbulence simulations, ranging in accuracy from $10^{-6}$ to $10^{-8}$. This energy retention allowed for the successful simulation of wave-number ranges extending into the sub-Michaelis-Menten regime, which might be achieved in three-dimensional scenarios as well with sufficiently high numbers of spatial grid points. Numerical solutions for the Balitsky and kinetic wave-kinetic equation frequency spectra were also derived. In particular, our solutions for the Balitsky equation frequency spectrum showed minimal dependence on the modulation wavenumber, while our solutions for the wave-kinetic equation frequency spectrum showed frequency-scaled, cubic-behavior, density-modulated spectra that are consistent with observed numerical data. An energy preservation law was also verified in this context. In a related matter, our solutions for the Balitsky equation frequency spectrum showed a significant, unstability-related, decay rate increase as the modulation wavenumber approaches a critical, double value, which corresponds to the Michaelis-Menten frequency scale. Large-scale real-world graph analysis necessitates novel algorithms that can accommodate the inherent complexities and scales inherent in these networks. The task of identifying the largest independent sets within these graphs is particularly significant, as max-weight independent sets can be considered a variant of the maximum independent set problem. Research has shown that an algorithm incorporating iterative graph normalization and a maximum independent set solution, applied in succession, can be used to solve the max-weight independent set problem. This method not only provides an efficient solution but also one that can be easily parallelized for enhanced computational performance. The maximum independent set problem, when solved using a brute-force approach that involves removing the most heavily weighted vertices, can, however, result in sub-optimal outcomes if the vertex weights are inappropriately defined. This paper discusses the underlying concept of vertex weight definition and illustrates a sophisticated approach to defining weights that enables accurate solutions to the max-weight independent set problem. The resulting algorithm, which has been dubbed the parallel-weighted independent set solver, or PARWITS, utilizes a combination of graph normalization and an improved vertex weighting strategy. The improvement in PARWITS-2, which solves the max-weight independent set problem, is then demonstrated through experiments and analyses that compare it to leading solutions, including the celebrated Bron-Karpovsky-Lehmer algorithm for the maximum independent set problem. The results indicate that PARWIS-2 is capable of producing accurate and efficient solutions that outperform existing methods. The paper also explores the theoretical bounds of PARWIS-2 by approximating its accuracy and time complexity using the known properties and parameters of random graphs. The analysis and case studies further highlight the operational effectiveness of PARWIS-2 in real-world settings. The paper also includes a companion repository that contains the source code, test data, and research results, which can be accessed via the given link. Recent discoveries of solar-type active binary star systems have uncovered unique radio-emitting objects, likely resulting from the interstellar medium's chaotic low-frequency radio emissions. Researchers have been interested in examining the low-frequency radio properties of these binary systems to gain insight into their unique radio-behavior. One such binary system, CR Draconis, composed of a K-type main-sequence star and a M-type anaught dwarf, has been observed emitting X-ray and microwave radiation. Using multiple decades of data collected from Penticton Observatory, researchers found that CR Draconis displays continuous low-frequency electron-cyclotron maser emission, in contrast to other flare stars, which typically exhibit periodicities tied to binary system rotation. Calculations indicated that CR Draconis' corona rotates once every 21.598 days, which researchers speculatively explain by considering the effects of Galactic plane passage and interactions between stellar wind and surrounding interstellar medium. Researchers found that CR Draconis' low-frequency emissions exhibit a 10% level of variability, which researchers compared to other flare stars, suggesting that the electron-cyclotron maser mechanism is the primary source of radio emissions in this binary system. Moreover, researchers observed a relatively small ratio of circular polarization in these emissions, which researchers compared to other flare stars, suggesting that CR Draconis' radiation mechanisms may differ. Researchers suggested that CR Draconis' constant low-frequency emissions may be the result of a stable stellar wind interacting with the surrounding interstellar medium, which researchers hypothesize could lead to the observed galactic plane periodicities. Researchers found that the star's coronal mass would need to be significantly larger than its actual value to explain the observed pulsation period, which researchers speculatively attribute to the star's magnetic field playing a role in generating the observed low-frequency emissions. Researchers propose that CR Draconis' population could represent a previously unaccounted for component of radio-emitting active stars in the Galactic plane, which researchers speculate may be related to the star's evolutionary state. Many current avatar visualization approaches rely on marking important locations, such as joints, and tracing the surfaces they define in 3D space. However, the conventional 2D rendering of these joints and surfaces can make the visualization appear stiff and inaccurate, such as when showing a character with its arm stretched, even if the arm is not actually stretched in the 3D environment. To overcome this problem, we have created a new method of visualization that effectively projects a fully articulated 3D model into 2D space in a way that is both realistic and informative. This new approach, which we call ANR, allows the creation of detailed, high-quality 2D animations of characters and objects that cater to a wide range of user needs. In addition to supporting both animated and static models, our method also makes it easy to view 3D models that have been captured or designed by others, essentially providing a standard platform for 3D creators to showcase their work in 2D. We have demonstrated the capabilities of our approach through multiple examples and highlighted its potential applications and future areas of improvement. This work is particularly useful in fields and applications involving virtual and augmented realisms, such as virtual reality and human-computer interaction. It can also serve as a basis for developing tools and interfaces that facilitate modeling, animation, and interaction across various domains and industries. To enable seamless collaboration and distribution of 3D models, we have created a user-friendly 2D sharing option that leverages the ANR method. This allows various stakeholders to view, interact, and use 3D models that have been created with animation and physics, providing a more immersive and engaging experience. Similar to other popular 3D software packages like Blender, our approach makes it easy for users to create and customize 2D animations and visuals. To facilitate modeling and animation, we have developed a user-friendly interface for adjusting 3D models and creating custom visuals. This includes an animation editor for designing and previewing animations and a model viewer for visualizing and customizing 3D models in 2D. To enhance user experience and improve accessibility, we have created a web-based platform for sharing and interacting with 3D models using the ANR method. This platform allows standard web browsing to generate and view 2D animations of 3D models in real-time. Our capacity to interpret context relies on the subtle connections between visual details, both in their literal meaning and in relation to other elements within our field of view. While researchers have made considerable progress in creating AI models that can recognize objects within images, these systems frequently prioritize isolated details over understanding global relationships between these objects. In our research, we investigate the effect of severe image transformations on both human and machine vision, focusing on the abilities of individuals with and without autism as well as deep learning-based visual detection models. Our study includes 24 different types of image transformations, 8 involving significant changes and 16 involving minor alterations, to assess their impact on performance. Our findings indicate that individuals with and without autism, as well as typical controls, react differently to these transformations, particularly to those affecting their overall visual experience. Interestingly, our results also show that both human and machine vision exhibit greater variability in response to minor transformations than in response to transformative changes. In addition to the experiments with individuals, we employed a computational analysis to assess the effect of these transformations on the performance of AI models. Our study provides valuable insights that can inform design decisions, particularly those involving accessible and inclusive design of AI systems that can function effectively in diverse contexts. Lastly, our findings also highlight the significance of the 7th Sustainable Development Goal, particularly in terms of technological advancements that can benefit or hinder human experience depending on their design. Our study presents computational findings using the Dolls House cluster quantum Monte Carlo technique to examine the properties of a two-dimensional, trapped cluster magnet. We found that the behavior of a simulated model closely mimics the characteristics of a lattice structure consisting of two different sizes of clusters linked together, consisting of either three (trimer) or six (tetramer) spins in a row. By changing the inter-cluster connections relative to the clusters' individual spin interactions, a phase transition is induced, shifting the system from an ordered state at low connection strengths to a partially ordered state. As the inter-cluster connections strengthen and their interactions equalize, the system transitions into a state where the trimer units align in a specific arrangement within a lattice pattern formed by the bonds between the clusters. Our results show that the findings using the Dolls House method complement existing calculations based on the density matrix renormalization group method. Furthermore, based on these results, a proposed phase diagram for a similar model investigated by Dergachev et al. has been revised. At equal interactions between cluster edges and corners, the phase boundary between the ordered and partially-ordered states exhibits a more gradual transition than previously suggested. Our study's findings using the Dolls House method also agree with more recent calculations using the vertex quantum Monte Carlo technique that directly sampled Bose-Einstein condensation of dimers at half-filling. Our research demonstrates the utility of the Dolls House method in simulating the ground states of more complex, two-dimensional quantum systems with multiple interactions. Recent research has highlighted pre-trained language models' effectiveness on various downstream NLP tasks via the use of prompts. A specific challenge in this area involves developing efficient, task-instantiation methods that take advantage of pre-trained model capabilities. We introduce the concept of Meta-tuning on Dataset and Prompt Assemblies (MPAs) as a solution to address this challenge. This approach first applies model inference to a finite set of NLP datasets and associated prompts, and then performs meta-learning to identify a task-agnostic language model modification strategy that can be applied broadly. This modification strategy can then be used to improve the model's performance on a wide range of NLP tasks, including tasks with very limited available data. Additionally, we propose the idea of Zero-shot Assembly Tracking (ZST), which allows the model to accurately keep track of referenced entities in applicable datasets. The proposed MPAs framework is successfully demonstrated through its application to the ZhMoDL model family, which was developed for multiple Chinese datasets. As a result, the enhanced model is found to be particularly effective not only on datasets it was originally trained on,  but also on other, unrelated datasets, and even with very limited (5 examples) available data. Furthermore, the model is found to perform well on ZST, allowing the user to know which entities the model is referring to when it writes "zero-shot". The research highlights the importance of developing a set of guidelines to ensure that prompt design facilitates model adaptation and promotes understanding of the task at hand. These findings were published in a recent paper, which can be accessed via the provided URL. They are also being further developed in my current PhD research. A new kinetic model, the $\nu$-model, is proposed to simplify the complex calculations associated with Boltzmann's collision operator in rarefied monatomic gas simulations. By integrating relaxation-time approximation, the $\nu$-model's collision frequency becomes velocity-dependent, thereby incorporating essential collision characteristics from Boltzmann's equation, while also reflecting the influence of the target velocity distribution function, akin to the Shakhov model. Following numerical simulations of a linear pipe and a mixed flow near its critical point, the velocity-dependent collision frequency was adjusted to achieve compatible temperature dependencies and optimal collision characteristics. As a result, the model's performance was enhanced, resulting in improved velocity space microcirculation and accurate pressure comparisons with the solution of the Boltzmann equation, along with refined macroscopic properties. Furthermore, the models with velocity-dependent collision frequency were successfully applied to simulate thermal creep and slip phenomena. The velocity-dependent collision frequency was also successfully integrated into the Shakhov model as an additional iteration step, enabling the optimization of the model's performance using the iterative iteration- Shakhov model. The results of the simulations indicate that the velocity-dependent collision frequency is sensitive to the target velocity distribution function, thereby allowing for accurate simulation of rarefied gas flows with varied temperature dependencies and surface conditions. As a result, the kinetic models with velocity-dependent collision frequency are effective tools for researching rarefied gas flows, particularly in cases with strong temperature gradients and slip and creep contributions. Natural Language Processing systems, essential for real-world applications, frequently lack sufficient data for successful deployment. Researchers have explored diverse methods to mitigate this limitation, such as transfer learning and data generation techniques. Nevertheless, these approaches often struggle when applied to certain tasks, like understanding the meaning of questions in visual question-answering systems. To address this issue, a novel approach known as Data-Efficient Naturalized Semantic Interpreters (DENSI) has been developed. DENSI leverages self-supervised learning and its superiority over a supervised approach is demonstrated on the task of visual question answering, requiring question meaning comprehension, using the CLEVR dataset. With a substantial reduction in image and human-annotated question-answer data, DENSI achieves significant improvements over existing techniques. Moreover, a related paper introduces a new CLEVR-based dataset to evaluate the performance of visual question answering systems, known as iCLEVR, requiring a substantial amount of data for accurate system deployment. Experimental results on iCLEVR demonstrate that DENSI outperforms other approaches by a large margin. Notably, a system enhanced with DENSI's naturalized semantic interpreter component retains 80% of its performance even when the training data is limited to a mere 1 percent of the original amount. The proposed framework with DENSI enables successful deployment on large and critical tasks such as visual question answering in the real world. The project's code and datasets are publicly available at: https://github.com/wohokomah/densi and https://wohokomah.github.io/iCLEVR. A newly discovered star, KPD 1946+4452B, is likely a binary black hole system containing a 3.7 day M6V+M7E active galactic nucleus. Following a significant drop in 2019, B's variability significantly increased in 2020, reaching nearly 50% and causing some to speculate that the system may have experienced a major outburst. We present detailed observations of B's extraordinary variability, totaling 207 days, accompanied by photometry from 1996-2021 and radial velocity measurements from 1998-2021. The most plausible explanation for B's behavior is that the binary star system experienced a type II quasi-periodic eruption, similar to that seen in SS 433 in 2011, and possibly again in 2019 and 2020. This interpretation is supported by combining our data with previously collected radial velocity information and by modeling the system as the known binary black hole system, SS 433/W43. The resulting analysis suggests that the binary's orbital period remains at 6.5 days, while the variability could be the result of both black hole ejections and pre-existing material degradation over the course of the 2020 eruption. The degradation may have been caused by the action of winds or shocks from the eruption itself. The estimated mass of the ejected object is 0.1-0.3 solar masses, placing its accretion rate at 5 x 10^-5 to 1.5 x 10^-3 solar masses per year. The spectrum of the ejected object is likely dominated by the emission of shocks, as seen in supernovae, possibly accompanied by the emission of continuous radiation from the accretion process. The failed tidal disruption of the binary's star by a supermassive black hole in 2019 appears to be the most plausible explanation for the eruption. The resulting radiation from the accretion process may have powered the previously seen multi-wavelength flares. Several federated learning frameworks have been created to enable the use of distributed data for training machine learning models while maintaining device data privacy. This paper examines the use of federated learning for nonlinear regression tasks. We review several algorithms for solving the federated learning optimization problem and compare their performance using both synthetic and real-world data. We also propose an asynchronous version of the Federated Averaged Gradient algorithm that enables models to be deployed quickly in scenarios with numerous devices and demonstrates comparable performance to current methods. To further improve the trading relationship between model accuracy and communication efficiency and device participation, we propose a resource-based asynchronous federated learning framework that allows the selection of the optimal number of participating devices and the optimal number of iterations for each round of Federated Averaged Gradient by considering the trade-off between model loss and communication costs. We also introduce the Asynchronous Federated Averaged Gradient algorithm with the Conjugate Gradient method as the local solver, which provides a balance between efficiency, scalability, and fairness for participating devices. We evaluate the performance of the proposed framework using real-world data for nonlinear regression tasks and demonstrate its effectiveness. Finally, we outline future research directions for several applications, including but not limited to nonlinear regression. The code for our implementation of the proposed framework is provided in the 'NPTK Resources for Federated Learning' repository. \\ \\ The paper's major contributions are: \\  The proposed framework achieves an execution speedup of 2-3 orders of magnitude when compared to the current best federated learning algorithms for nonlinear regression tasks using real-world data. \\  The asynchronous version of the Federated Averaged Gradient algorithm maintains a performance comparable to several current methods for federated learning. \\  The proposed framework reduces communication costs by enabling the selection of the optimal number of participating devices and the optimal number of iterations for each round of Federated Averaged Gradient in the resource-constrained environment. \\  The code for our implementation was provided in the 'NPTK Resources for Federated Learning' repository at https://github.com/NationalTechnologies/Federated-Learning. Constructing an accurate depression detection system from social media data is a daunting task, largely due to the lack of a definitive definition and diagnostic standard, as well as the vast variability in depression symptoms and presentations. To tackle this issue, this research establishes a social media dataset comprising 402 online posts from individuals who have self-identified as depressed, in addition to 802 non-depressed posts for comparison. To optimize depression detection, this work employs a novel deep neural network architecture, which can automatically identify relevant social media content and refine its representation for better classification results. Our analysis demonstrates that social media platforms can be valuable tools in detecting early signs of depression, particularly in the form of informal conversations. Furthermore, we found that depression-related cues on social media are often characterized by a range of emotions, rather than a single predominant one. Our empirical results indicate that a social media post can be classified as depressed or non-depressed with high accuracy, as young individuals are more likely to engage in conversational online discussions about their emotions. A stick-slip phenomenon characterized by low-velocity, high-force oscillations is a well-documented behavior observed in systems governed by Coulomb friction. In the course of a motion, if a system's velocity drops below the threshold required for sliding, a stick-state is entered, only to be transitioned out of it when the necessary force threshold is reached, allowing sliding to resume. This cycle repeatedly occurs under certain dynamic conditions. Although the stick-slip oscillations typically converge in models that account for frictional history, their persistent occurrence in numerous practical applications remains a source of considerable interest and concern. This paper explores the dynamic evolution during convergent motion and demonstrates that the distinct phases of the dynamic convergence process are marked by a sequence of stick-slip events, thus providing a rigorous mathematical confirmation of this phenomenon. Consequently, the net effect of these oscillations is a velocity deceleration, ultimately resulting in a final stopping state that is determined by the force of friction. The numerical validation of our findings was performed utilizing a model consisting of an inertial mass, subject to both frictional and viscous damping forces. Our results suggest that a particular condition, namely when a system's velocity decreases monotonically, is sufficient for the reliable termination of stick-slip oscillations and thus enables the prediction of successful convergence in various practical scenarios involving multiple degrees of freedom. Modeling these intentions is crucial for providing user-centric suggestions and protecting their privacy. This study introduces a method to represent user goals as latent variables, which are updated incrementally as the user's behavior evolves over time. The model's architecture consists of two key components: 1) a representation learning system that extracts features from user and item attributes, and 2) a sequential decoding network that infers user goals at each subsequent time step. The proposed approach performs well on real datasets from a sequential recommendation service, demonstrating up to a 52% improvement in predictive accuracy compared to a baseline benchmark. Evaluations on actual users also reveal more diverse and natural-looking goal distributions in comparison. The study showcases the impact of modeling user intentions on the performance of a recommender system. The approach can be particularly beneficial in applications where users incur costs when interacting with recommendations. The Fuchsian equation's singular point at $x=0$ exhibits a very specific behavior related to its monodromy matrix, showing a transition from a resonant to a non-resonant state as $x$ changes sign. The source itself can be expressed in terms of Bessel functions for $x\geq0$ or alternating Bessel functions for $x<0$. The paper provides an expression for the solution in terms of a specific product containing the Bessel functions for $x\geq0$, highlighting its connection to a singular hypergeometric equation related to an irregular singularity. The solution can then be expressed using a similar product for $x<0$, along with a suitable connection formula that allows the solution to be extended across the singular point by pairing up resonant and non-resonant behaviors. The solution's behavior when expanded in a power series around $x=0$ or in a Laurent series around $x\neq0$ is also compared, with both series being equally non-resonant. This study categorizes COVID-19 into mild or severe based on clinical features, automatically generating a diagnosis from patient information. A BERT-based neural network model is employed for feature extraction, followed by a Deep Neural Network to make predictions. A recently established framework for measuring the susceptibility of self-supervised speech models to adversarial attacks has been introduced. This framework enables the comprehensive evaluation of model resistance using two distinct metrics: the first being robustness to perceptually similar inputs, and the second being the gap in asymptotic performance between the adversarially trained model and its non-adversarially trained counterpart. Notably, the second metric is influenced by the level of perturbation introduced during adversarial training, with higher perturbation levels leading to a greater gap in performance. To address this concern, a novel technique called "within-distance constraint" was developed to mitigate the dependence on perturbation levels by enforcing a maximum distance threshold for the target input's closest sample during adversarial training. By imposing this constraint, the self-supervised model is forced to avoid developing defenses that rely on separating data into distinct classes. Experimental results on Speech Commands Vw and YouTube-Librispeech have demonstrated the effectiveness of this technique in comparing the robustness of different self-supervised models, while also highlighting the significant impact of model architecture and dataset on asymptotic performance robustness. This framework and its methods are anticipated to facilitate the evaluation and development of robust self-supervised speech models. DXs have gained popularity among users with diverse preferences, including those seeking anonymity, high levels of liquidity, and low transaction fees. We investigate the mechanisms and characteristics that govern DX function and provide practical applications to help DX administrators and developers in maintaining their platforms, as evidenced by our successful real-world predictions of DX price fluctuations and liquidity changes. While DXs have achieved notable success, our analysis also identifies potential challenges to their continued growth and adoption. In cases where data is incomplete, researchers often use imputation or regression methods to infer parameters. The E-value metric, which evaluates the precision of parameter estimates in the presence of missing data, can be applied broadly and has been largely studied under the assumption of complete data. Our objective is to explore the relationship between the E-value when data is missing and when data is not missing, with a particular focus on identifying patterns that indicate whether the E-value is informative about missing data analysis. To this end, we will examine a straightforward missing data scenario and analyze the conditions under which the E-value when data is missing reflects the E-value when data is not missing, with a focus on applying these findings to real-world studies. The results will lead to recommendations for the assessment of Bayesian analysis sensitivity in the presence of missing data. The methodology will be illustrated using data from a HIV trial. The proposed methodology and analysis will be carried out using R software, which will also be made freely available through CRAN. The latter part of this dissertation will involve an extension of this research to consider the selection of relevant variables in the presence of missing data within a Bayesian context. The approach will be based on a principle similar to the E-value but more appropriate for the analysis of missing data, which is the informative strength of a univariate regression coefficient. The conditions under which the informative strength when data is missing reflects the situation where data is not missing will be studied and recommendations for the assessment of missing data analysis sensitivity will be suggested. The approach will be applied in the context of a collaborative qualitative infectious disease study. The missing data analysis sensitivity assessment will be made using freely available R software that also handles missing data entry, data imputation, and various missing data analysis methods including regression and multiple imputation. The latter will also allow for the calculation of the E-value metric to compare the refractory period distribution parameters of patients with HIV, which will be estimated using a survival model. The relevant R software will be made freely available through CRAN. The latter part of this dissertation will involve an extension of this research to consider the selection of relevant features in the presence of missing data within a Bayesian context, which is based on a principle similar to the E-value but more appropriate for the analysis of missing data, which is the informative strength of a univariate regression coefficient. The approach will be denoted the I-value. The conditions under which the I-value when data is missing reflects the situation where data is not missing will be studied and recommendations for the analysis of missing data sensitivity assessment will be suggested

Understanding universal properties of a critical quantum spin chain model requires accurately capturing universal characteristics present in conformal field theory. Researchers have relied on numerical methods, specifically using finite size scaling, to extract information about conformal field theory's central charges from numerical data. Meanwhile, the theory of conformal field theory has advanced significantly since the early numerical studies. This work attempts to bridge the gap between new theoretical developments and numerical research by applying recent advances in understanding conformal field theory to numerical simulations. The approach presented here generalizes a method for calculating universal terms in the energy spectrum, where the energy spectrum is represented as a sum of the minimal energy spectrum and universal terms. The calculated universal terms are based on the norm squares of local operators' wavefunction representations. Importantly, the calculated terms are independent of model specifics and are thus easily accessible. To demonstrate the approach's effectiveness, the researchers applied it to the Haagerup model. The new method allows for a straightforward conformal field theory analysis of the time-evolution operator's end-to-end correlations. As a result, the approach provides direct numerical evidence for a long-standing conjecture involving the Haagerup model's central charge and Mandelstam-Two-Point Correlation Function's end-to-end amplitude. Moreover, the approach's results confirm that the Haagerup model's universal terms in the energy spectrum are independent of model specifics. The approach's applicability to various spin chain models with chiral properties suggests that the approach could be adapted to these models as well. Given the approach's results and the provided step-by-step guidelines, researchers hope that other spin chain models can be studied in a similar manner. The numerical data and code used in this research have been made publicly available. The researcher hopes that other researchers can use this approach to study the end-to-end amplitudes in various systems and the wavefunction intersections in one-dimensional systems. The approach's results and the numerical data and code used in this research have been shared on the repository: https://github.com/yannguoa/bulk-end-correlations. Automated part-of-speech (POS) annotation is a crucial step in linguistics research, typically performed after text cleaning and tokenization, to enable further analysis and categorization of words and their contexts. Although advancements have improved the accuracy of POS annotation for contemporary languages, this accuracy significantly decreases when dealing with historical languages, due to limited frame-based models and the absence of comprehensive corpora for model development. Existing machine learning approaches to POS annotation for historical languages are also hindered by tokenization and typographical issues. Set-valued output, which accounts for multiple word sense ambiguities and tokenization mistakes in annotation, has been found beneficial in POS annotation for historical languages. In this study, we examine how set-valued output can enhance POS annotation by allowing for consideration of multiple word sense ambiguities and typological errors. We examine three corpus datasets from Finnish, French, and Czech, and propose a novel technique for set-valued output POS annotation. Our experimental results indicate that incorporating set-valued output leads to improved accuracy and robustness in POS annotation, particularly in contexts with high word sense ambiguity and typological error frequency. Our proposed methodology also demonstrates comparable or superior performance to existing annotation techniques, both set-valued and frame-based. Our analysis suggests that incorporating typological variables as features can further improve the accuracy of POS annotation. Our experimental results also demonstrate the benefits of using translation matrices to translate typological features from one language to another. Our work has the potential to facilitate set-valued output POS annotation for a broader range of languages. It may also be applied to other natural language processing tasks that require accurate annotation of linguistic features. Our paper presents a novel theoretical contribution by generalizing the concept of set-valued output to multiple authors, incorporating typological variables, and proposing a translation matrix to facilitate set-valued output POS annotation. Our experimental results provide empirical support for the concept of set-valued output POS annotation. Our proposal of translation matrices as features to account for the differences in orthography, grammar, and syntax between languages is also justified by our experimental results. Our work has the potential to be replicated by other researchers in the field. Our paper contains a list of further readings on the topics of translation matrices, part-of-speech annotation, and typological features. Our experimental results indicate that incorporating typological variables as features can further improve the accuracy of POS annotation. Our paper contains a list of variables used in our features file. Our experimental results provide a detailed analysis of the strengths and weaknesses of set-valued output POS annotation for three corpus datasets.

The increased reliance on automation technologies stems from their greater precision, capacity, and capability to process vast amounts of data expeditiously. Moreover, automation has a profound impact on the efficiency of data transmission and information exchange among disparate entities. In the context of the smart city initiative, numerous automated systems have been implemented to expedite the processing and transmission of data, encompassing smart infrastructure, transportation, healthcare, and city governance. In particular, city administrators utilize automated systems to create detailed specifications for tender documents, a process aimed at streamlining and standardizing this process. Nonetheless, automatic translation and data exchange remain significant challenges across the smart city spectrum. To address this issue, we introduce an innovative approach, the Smart Assistant, designed to facilitate the automatic transformation of City Requirements from natural language into formal specification using $\mathcal{C}$. Formally speaking, the Smart Assistant can generate a formal $\mathcal{C}$-City Requirements model from an informal City Requirements document, thus alleviating the current reliance on manual specification creation. To validate the efficacy of the Smart Assistant, we employed two quantitative measures: (i) the optimization of formal specifications for efficient data transmission and (ii) the comparison of generated models with expert specifications. Furthermore, we conducted an initial experiment on City Requirements obtained via a content analysis of publicly available smart city tender documents, comprising 3 experts' specifications and a total of 122 documents. To accomplish this task, we utilized the properties of the $\mathcal{C}$ language, namely the exploitation of data, abstraction operators, and the application of a set of predefined requirements. The resulting generated models, totalizing 44 entities, 97 roles, and 179 properties, enabled the calculation of the optimization of formal specifications as 73.42% and the comparison of generated models with expert specifications reached 87% of accuracy. Ultimately, the Smart Assistant has been validated through the demonstration of its practical application in delivering formal specifications to tender documents automation to the smart city domain. Specifically, the Assistant has been successfully implemented in two key use cases: the smart governance of cities, particularly in the context of Milan Smart Governance, and the smart transportation systems of the city of Rome. Consequently, the proposed technology has far-reaching implications and can be adapted to various other use cases across the smart city spectrum. Its eventual adaptation and successful deployment across multiple domains highlight the necessity to consider automation as a crucial element in smart city integration and to address the automatic translation and data exchange challenges inherent to the composition of diverse automated systems within the smart city initiative.

In the past decade, superconducting quantum devices have rapidly advanced and are now close to realizing a crucial element of quantum computing technology: large-scale quantum error correction. Furthermore, a recent study found that an innovative method, the hidden inverses protocol, can effectively correct quantum error at an unprecedented scale. This new technique was first demonstrated in ion trap systems and was later adapted for use in superconducting quantum devices. Researchers have suggested that the latter devices would require a modified version of the protocol due to differing error characteristics. This proposed modification has, however, introduced significant hurdles in successfully implementing the error correction technique using current quantum devices. Therefore, a detailed analysis of the modified protocol as applied to superconducting quantum devices is needed to assess its feasibility. This study undertakes that task by introducing a key concept -- the inverse control ratio -- to evaluate performance, introducing a detection probability of the hidden inverse and examining the practical applicability of this error correction technique using current SQDs. Our findings indicate that, despite the differing error characteristics in SQDs, this class of devices is well-suited for implementing the hidden inverses protocol. This suitability is due to a unique property where the performance of this technique in SQDs cannot be described solely by the average performance metric as previously suggested, but is instead influenced by both this average value and its variability. This conclusion was verified through a series of numerical simulations both in the classical framework and using a quantum device designed using quantum noise modeling. This research provides valuable insights into the development and optimization of this novel error correction technique. It provides, for example, specific guidelines on the number of encodings/decodings needed to successfully apply the error correction method as well as suggestions for improving this technique's performance. In doing so, we establish that a category with binary joins is equivalent to a poset if and only if it has an initial object, with the corresponding hom-sets representing the relations in the poset. This poset is then shown to be a complete lattice if and only if the category's joins are extensive within it. Recently, Contrasting pre-trained image and text embeddings through Visual-Language Pre-training has received significant interest due to its capacity to learn universal visual and textual transformations. Nevertheless, its current deployment is largely limited to supporting tasks which require a direct visual description, such as image retrieval and localizing. In order to effectively carry out complex operations like image captioning and visual question answering, where visual focus guidance is crucial, we suggest employing a unified visual-textual transformer that combines clipping with visual-directional pointing. This proposal is referred to as VT-CLIP and it significantly outperforms the existing best approach in all the mentioned applications. Notably, our implementation is based on the widely-used CLIP model, and we directly train it without requiring any additional fusion modules or fine-tuning processes, making our solution relatively straightforward to execute. Thorough experiments and analysis are conducted to demonstrate the main contributions of our paper. They involve understanding the role of visual-directional pointers in bridging the gap between CLIP's image and text spaces by identifying the visually-attended text span during visual-question answering, and also in generating detailed image descriptions by visually-annotating the relevant text segments. Furthermore, we explore the potential of CLIP-based models to support multi-modal coherent discussions by identifying the agreed upon text phrases during visual-based conversations. The code for our models is now openly available on GitHub. By leveraging VT-CLIP, we aim to take the first step towards developing a unified cross-modal cross-form framework that integrates various modalities of different forms, and we strongly advise re-training a PLM like CLIP with visual pointer objectives to release the constraints of its current image-text alignment space. This re-release allows the PLM to naturally identify the visually-attended text spans during visual question answering and also in generating image descriptions. However, we strongly advise not releasing the CLIP model itself. The code for our models is now openly available on GitHub.
